strength: Very concrete and fits our capacity exactly: 12 writer slots and 3 dated developer days. Week 1 runs day by day with a ready title, meta and page outline in our voice, and the numbers are right (3.2% vs 0.25%, 38% to paid).
mistake: It says to leave decaying blog posts live and unchanged instead of merging or redirecting them into pages that convert. The projection for move 4 ('3 to 35') is muddled.
to10: Add a consolidate-or-redirect step for dead posts, explain the cookie-page projection clearly, and give a month-by-month trial forecast rather than only the end-state range.

strength: The trials-per-1,000-clicks table is a clear way to see the data. It covers more ground: a GA4 migration page for Maya's old-data fear, an agency page, a /compare hub, and merging or redirecting dead posts.
mistake: The projections assume top-3 rankings (9% CTR on /vs-google-analytics), so the 175-trial ceiling looks optimistic. Month 3 leaves competitors and posts undecided, and the audit adds work outside our stated capacity.
to10: Use more conservative ranges tied to realistic position gains, name the Month 3 pages now, plan refreshes for the other vs pages, and fit the audit inside the team's time.

strength: The page is tightly built around recruiting. It shows the seat math with a sharp comparison (733 vs 12 paid seats per 1,000 signups), moves routing up and security to sit right before a 4-field demo form, and includes a real sample-size plan for the test.
mistake: The hero says 'back and forth' instead of Priya's own 'email tennis', and the PTO promise only shows up in variant B. The sample-size math uses the 3.1% homepage signup rate as the baseline for a different metric.
to10: Put Priya's 'email tennis' phrase and the PTO-aware round robin into the hero. Vary the buttons in a few middle sections so it doesn't read as eight identical 'Book a demo' asks. Base the sample size on a recruiting-page baseline.

strength: The hero is built on Priya's 'email tennis' with round robin that skips people who are off. The bracket placeholders handle unverified facts honestly, and it explains clearly why the two heroes test different ideas.
mistake: It mixes 'Get started' buttons into a team page where the brief says teams get 'Book a demo'. Security sits three sections away from the demo form. The '3-4 emails per interview' figure is invented and not from our data.
to10: Use 'Book a demo' throughout and move the security section next to the demo form. Cut the invented email count. Size the test duration instead of just saying 'two weeks'.

strength: Opens with the three numbers, admits the forecast miss in the first line, and sets out the $2.2M burn rise in a clear table.
mistake: Customer A comes second under the AI-builder story, and the asks only appear at the very bottom. The derived claim that the $0.9M is 'roughly 9 points of margin' is shaky, and it says so itself: it adds up to more than the actual 7-point drop.
to10: Put Customer A first among the bad news, preview the asks in the first screen, and give the 48-hour fix a ship date. Drop the margin-attribution math that doesn't reconcile.

strength: Everything the lead partner needs is in the first screen: three numbers, the miss, what we need and by when. Customer A leads the bad news. The fix has a ship date, and the asks come with ready-to-forward blurbs.
mistake: It states the New York base as decided, which I still have to confirm. Asks 1 and 3 don't say whether they are for the lead partner or the angels. It also runs close to the length limit.
to10: Name who each ask is for. Add Customer A's likely effect on NRR. Trim slightly to stay safely under 700 words.

strength: Precise targeting with a clear leave-out table. The idea of timing the sequence around their close, so step 4 lands before month-end, is something I hadn't thought of.
mistake: Step 1 already asks for a 20-minute call, which is a heavy ask for a first touch given what the pilot showed about calendar asks. The close-window rule can also delay sends past the fresh pricing flag.
to10: Use a lower-friction ask in step 1. Reconcile the close-window timing with sending soon after the flag. Make clear the 4,100 'left out' count also excludes unflagged Controllers.

strength: Tight emails with low-friction one-word reply asks. Weekly loading tied to the data tool's flags. Honest expectation logic that refuses to multiply the two gains.
mistake: The 'all 1,900 loaded' projection of 55 meetings assumes every Controller will trigger a pricing change, which is optimistic. Step 2 slips in a product claim, and step 4 crams in an either/or question.
to10: Size the projection by the expected weekly flag volume, not the full 1,900. Cut the product line from step 2. Add one bolder test idea.

strength: The hard parts come right after the opening: hours, a weekend rotation of 'one in six, about 8 or 9 a year', and working alone. A local-time table makes the Asia-Pacific need concrete, and $82,000 is in the title.
mistake: 45% of the scorecard weight sits on interview rows, which leans on the stage our own data says predicts little (0.11). The post also never shows the customer email applicants will answer, so the form isn't ready to launch.
to10: Raise the writing rows to about 50 to 60% and cut the interview weight. Include the actual sample customer email in the post. Trim the reviewer-hours table so the plan reads faster.

strength: The post includes a real-feeling HEY lockout email to answer, which makes the application exercise usable today. Writing gets 50% of the scorecard, there is a clear 4.0 offer rule, and the welcome to career changers sounds just like us.
mistake: The weekend rotation sits under its own heading rather than leading the hard parts. The extra 'why this job' answer adds reading time without being scored. The post lists only one set of local times, which leaves out Sydney and Tokyo applicants.
to10: Fold the weekend rotation into the top of the hard parts. Add a short local-time table. Drop or score the 'why' question. Add the structured interview questions Output 1 provided.

strength: Every number checks out: 60% of Semrush losses are agencies, Lite is 70% of churn, and multi-site AWT is 42% of free conversions. The five moves form one agency play: the report beta, the multi-site onboarding, and a free report in AWT that builds the habit before agencies ever compare tools.
mistake: The Lite usage-limit fix sits at #2 even though it is the cheapest and fastest money. The top summary also crowds 'do first', 'stop' and 'don't spend' together, which makes it a little dense for a grade-9 read.
to10: Make the Lite top-up the #1 quick win, or explicitly frame it as first money. Give the Move 3 and Move 5 tests one shared calendar. Add a dated source line for the survey claims.

strength: The clearest structure for me as reader: where we lose, where we don't, our biggest leak, the moves, and what not to do. It also has a sharp Lite retention stat: only 37% are left after 12 months.
mistake: Move 5, the link-data content studies, is the generic 'do more content' advice I didn't want. Move 1 also widens scope by pulling in client ad and analytics data, and its first step is 40 interviews rather than something we can ship this month.
to10: Replace Move 5 with something that compounds the agency bet, such as a free report in AWT. Keep the v1 report on existing Ahrefs data so it ships faster. Move the Lite fix up.

strength: The launch gates are hard-nosed and fit our data. Migration must be proven on 1,000 real setups, there is a one-step undo, and the staged rollout depends on ticket volume. Putting engineers on support during the freeze turns idle capacity into faster replies.
mistake: The X thread ships with broken placeholders ("Opens in  ms on a  Mac") and four extra posts, so it isn't paste-ready. The calendar also has no clear owner column, and creators get the build only two weeks before launch.
to10: Add owners to every row. Get creators the build a week earlier. Add success targets and a plan B. Tighten the X post into one finished post with real author credits.

strength: It opens with a clear decision and ties every step to our numbers. The ranking includes the retention math and totals. The dated calendar has owners and fits the freeze. It sets measurable targets against 2025 and has a plan B with triggers. This is what I'd hand the team on Monday.
mistake: The projection paragraph is a bit muddled, and it probably runs slightly over 1,200 words. The staged rollout is offered as an optional 'bolder move' when it arguably belongs in the gates.
to10: Make the staged update and a one-step settings restore hard gates. Simplify the projection to one line. Name the specific authors to credit in the X post.

strength: It targets the Essentials 8+ leak with a flat plan and a clear test with stop rules. It also takes on yearly billing honestly: it ships the visibility fix to everyone and shows that yearly helps retention but does not lift revenue within two quarters.
mistake: $99 is a big jump from the typical $64 bill. The math also leans on fairly optimistic upgrade rates, and the low case is near zero. The writing is dense with numbers, and the 'bolder move' section edges toward a second recommendation.
to10: Justify the $99/25-channel price point against the freelancer's actual bill, or test a lower price. Trim the number density for a grade-7 reader. Personalize the customer email with their current bill.

strength: Very clear and in our voice. The email shows the customer's own bill next to the new price, promises they can switch back, and uses no pressure. It has clean go and stop thresholds and states the Team move-down break-even plainly.
mistake: It treats yearly billing as an afterthought, offered only at the moment of switching, when that is our cheapest retention win. It also annualizes month-6 MRR into a '$276k a year' figure instead of showing cumulative revenue over two quarters for the board.
to10: Add the yearly-visibility fix for all customers and show six-month cumulative revenue against the board's window. Address the 15-channel cliff in the pricing itself.

strength: It plans all 24 posts with hooks, within capacity, and leads with sleep and narrator clips in the evening. The week 1 drafts use our customers' own words ('brain still on', 'replaying emails', 'quit by day three') in our warm voice.
mistake: It says no post needs review but does not plan a submission for borderline later posts like 'Awake at 2am'. It also tacks on a live-stream idea, which risks scope creep and pushes the length past 1,200 words.
to10: Flag which week 2 to 4 hooks could trigger review and batch-submit them on 16 November. Drop the bolt-on live idea to stay within length.

strength: It handles review timing cleanly by batch-submitting weeks 2 to 4 on 16 November. The success measures are sensible and include a caveat that the 5.9% narrator save rate comes from a small sample of 5 posts.
mistake: Weeks 2 to 4 get only one-line weekly angles, not post-level hooks, so the plan is less usable past week 1. Batch-submitting 18 posts on day one also puts unspoken pressure on the team.
to10: Add a 24-post hook grid like a real calendar, and say who writes the weeks 2 to 4 posts and when so the 16 November batch is realistic.

strength: A tight, calm series built on the two habits that predict retention. Email 3 branches by signup platform, Email 4 is a guilt-free inactivity check-in, and the drop list is backed by our own numbers.
mistake: The last slot goes to a Pro pitch instead of finishing the habit work. It also leans on a feature claim (time reminders are Pro) that I'd need to check, and users who never add a task never get the recurring-task email.
to10: Use email 5 to push whichever habit the user is missing. Add a day-based fallback so users who never add a task still get email 2. Include an at-a-glance table of sends and skips.

strength: The whole series serves the two habits. Email 5 sends only the missing step. There are fallback send days for every trigger, a clear at-a-glance table with skip rules, and measures sized to our volume (1,800 people a quarter per point).
mistake: The control group gets no onboarding emails at all, not even the welcome. That is a costly holdout. Pro also disappears from the series without a plan for revenue in the first month.
to10: Hold back a control group that keeps the old series, or a bare welcome only. Give a concrete post-day-30 Pro plan with its own measure. Trim a little to stay safely under 1,200 words.

strength: The decision and the numbers come first: 3.2% vs 0.25% conversion, the 13% fall in organic clicks, and what the lost blog clicks were worth. The week 1 plan is Monday-ready with a draft title, meta, and outline in our voice, and the plan includes rollback and measurement rules.
mistake: It tells the writer to leave decaying posts alone. It never says to merge or redirect them. It also makes no case for a GA4 data-migration page, which is Maya's biggest worry. It is also a little long for the 1,000-word cap.
to10: Add a stop-or-redirect rule for the decaying blog posts. Add a 'moving from GA4 without losing history' page for Maya. Trim to under 1,000 words. Keep the conservative trial forecast by month and the dated draft title and meta.

strength: Clean trials-per-1,000-clicks table and a well-ranked list with paid-customer figures. It adds a GA4 history page for Maya's main fear and a rule to merge or redirect dead posts, and every month is mapped to the 12-page limit.
mistake: The forecasts are optimistic. Moving /vs-google-analytics to a 9% CTR gives +100 trials, and the plan then calls the sum of these a 'ceiling'. Month 3 is vague ('pick two competitors'). The week 1 plan has no concrete title or meta draft. It also sends the draft to me for a facts check when I'm unavailable.
to10: Use realistic forecasts per month. Write the actual title and meta in week 1. Name the Month 3 pages. Cut the developer-day tasks to what one day can really hold. Keep the GA4 history page and the redirect rule.

strength: It picks recruiting with correct seat math and gives a complete test plan: one decisive metric, sample size, run length and a stopping rule. The page copy uses real numbers and no invented customers.
mistake: It runs well past the 1,000-word limit with extras nobody asked for (projection, 'bolder move'). The hero lacks Priya's 'email tennis' language, and the hero offers two actions at once, which breaks the one-action rule.
to10: Cut to the word limit, put Priya's own phrase in the hero, keep one action per section, and move the security proof up beside the first demo button.

strength: The hero uses the customer's own words ('No email tennis') and the segment case is crisp: 0.73 paid seats per signup against 0.17 for the next segment, plus 57% of new paid seats. Its 'why these two' note explains that the heroes test different ideas.
mistake: Several team-page buttons say 'Get started' instead of 'Book a demo', against brand rules. The deciding metric needs a 7-day first booking, so it is slow to call. It also adds a few unsupported claims (text reminders, 'three or four emails').
to10: Use 'Book a demo' on every team section, define a metric that can be read right away, add a sample size and run length, remove the unverified claims, and put security proof near the demo button.

strength: The top of the email gives the three numbers, the missed forecast and a one-line summary of the asks. Customer A and the margin story follow right after. The asks have named profiles, dates and copy-paste forwarding blurbs, which is exactly what the angels wanted.
mistake: It states that the VP role 'is now based in New York' as a settled decision. That is only an assumption, and it is flagged at the bottom rather than where it appears. It also never says that Customer A's exit will pull NRR down, and it gives no estimate of how much the 48-hour pause will save.
to10: Mark the New York decision as one to confirm. Add the expected NRR effect of Customer A's exit and a rough saving range for the 48-hour pause. Trim a few words so it sits comfortably under 700.

strength: It explains the burn increase in a clean table: $0.9M compute, $0.8M one-off and $0.5M hires. It also shows that nearly all the database growth came from AI-builder partners (direct up only 2.6%). Its third ask, on pricing partner traffic, is aimed at the lead partner and fits the real problem.
mistake: It says $0.9M on about $10.4M of monthly revenue is 'roughly 9 points of margin, more than the 7-point drop'. This confuses the reader, because it treats all of the compute rise as cost of goods sold without saying so. The line 'Ask 2 helps' is also awkward. The VP ask goes to 'everyone' with no named reader.
to10: Drop or properly explain the margin arithmetic. Put the asks summary near the top for the phone reader. Add forwardable blurbs for the intros. Give a rough saving range for the pause and say what Customer A's exit does to NRR.

strength: It leads with the call and then gives a complete, usable package: tight list rules, a link-free sequence built on the pricing-change and rev rec hook, send rules with an opt-out footer, reply handling, a subject test and an honest reply-rate floor.
mistake: The 12th-to-15th send window makes flags that fire during close wait, which cuts against the freshness of the pricing-change trigger. The 4.0% positive-reply figure is also scaled up rather than taken from the pilot. The step 1 ask is a 20-minute call, which is heavy for a first cold email.
to10: Drop the send-window delay or tie it to the weekly flag, use only pilot-backed positive-rate numbers, soften the step 1 ask, and check that the total stays within 900 words.

strength: The expected-reply-rate reasoning is the most honest of the two. It takes the pilot floor, explains why it does not multiply the two gains, gives per-100 and full-list numbers, and sets a check after 300 sends.
mistake: It invents assets and claims the brief did not supply: a one-page summary, three steps the team took, and Chargebee being built so finance and engineering share one setup. It also says "controllers tell me," which is false familiarity. Emails have no opt-out or address footer, and the proof is absent from step 3.
to10: Remove the invented assets and the product claim, add a compliance footer and reply handling, and offer a bolder test idea, all while staying within 900 words.

strength: Complete, usable package: post with local-time table and hard parts up front, a one-reply application with a costed reviewer-hours plan, and a scorecard with weights and 1/3/5 anchors tied to the data.
mistake: Writing carries only 55% of the weight (and interview rows 45%), so the 0.62 signal is not weighted as heavily as it should be. It also says 'two of the three recent hires' (a slight misstatement), and the post runs long and mixes in process detail, including a 'hear back within a week of each call' promise that was never in the brief.
to10: Weight writing 50% or more, trim interview rows, fix the leaver wording, and drop the invented timing promises. Keep the hour table and the post's plainness.

strength: Weights writing at 50%, with interview impression small, directly following the 0.62 vs 0.11 data. It puts a real sample customer email in the post, and its post is short, warm and candid, with salary on the first line and the weekend rotation in its own section.
mistake: Adds an unrequested 'longer written exercise' stage and a 'why this job' essay that adds reviewer work. The hours-saved estimate (70 hours) leaves out the extra stage and the first-pass cost is optimistic; the 4-and-5 re-read is only lightly costed.
to10: Cost the longer-exercise stage in reviewer hours, drop the 'why this job' question, and add a local-time table for more regions.

strength: Sound, checkable arithmetic: trials lost per 100, Lite as 70% of churned customers, and the 12-month Lite survival of 37%. It shows agencies are 27% of trials but 60% of Semrush losses, and that the Lite limit is the biggest self-inflicted leak. It also has a clear 'what we should not do' list.
mistake: Move 5 (content from our link data) is generic, with a one-line first step and a vague metric. The 'November 2026' date is invented. The Lite fix is placed second, and the output never calls it the fastest money.
to10: Drop the invented date and replace move 5 with something tied to the agency or Lite problems. Say outright that the Lite fix is the quickest cash win. Give each move a sharper metric and a concrete first step.

strength: It opens with a one-screen verdict (lose, tie, win, not a Semrush problem) plus a do-first, stop and don't-spend list. Every move has an owner, a first step and a metric. It links the agency report to the multi-site free accounts, and its bold fifth move is a free report inside Webmaster Tools.
mistake: The Lite top-up is ranked second rather than first, though it is probably the quickest win. It also loosely ties the top-up to the in-house price-jump complaint. Moves 4 and 5 are thinner on projected impact.
to10: Rank the Lite limit fix first or equal first, as the cheapest win. Give a firmer success target for move 4, and trim a few words so it sits safely under 1,100.

strength: Eight concrete go/no-go gates (1,000-user beta migration proof, undo, top-200 extension tests, support with engineers on shifts, staged rollout) and a dated timeline that covers all audiences and the freeze.
mistake: The X post puts several shortcuts and claims in a 5-post thread and the AI builder is shown in launch-day assets, which risks breaking the one-shortcut rule. The table also lists X above Hacker News but ranks by retained users inconsistently (X 3,740 is listed below authors 2,470). Product Hunt is also given its own day, which is fine, but the Show HN is written on launch day. There is also a blank speed placeholder.
to10: Fix the ranking order so it truly follows retained users, add owners to each calendar row, keep one shortcut per message, and trim the five-post thread to something the team can ship tomorrow.

strength: It opens with a clear decision, ties every move to the 2025 numbers, and gives an owner-assigned calendar that works backward from the freeze, with the author build going out 17 November so bugs are found before 1 December. Measures, plan B and the 10% wave add real management value.
mistake: Its projection mixes installs and retained users in a confusing way, and the 12-hour reply target is loosely supported. It also gives fewer pre-launch tests with real user numbers than Output 1 and has no beta for power users beyond the authors.
to10: Give a clearer retained-user projection, add a power-user beta for migration proof, and include a short speed number placeholder rule.

strength: It pairs one flat Agency plan for 8+ channel accounts with an honest yearly-billing fix. It shows low, mid and high revenue cases, a holdout test with three stop rules, and a clear admission that nothing from repricing the base can land inside the board's window.
mistake: The 'bolder move' on locking yearly prices adds a second idea to a brief that asked for one recommendation. The tables are dense and the text runs to the word limit. The 25-channel cap at $99 may also undercut Team more than the draft admits.
to10: Drop or shrink the bolder-move section. Spell out the month-6 math more simply so a small team can check it. State what share of Team 8+ accounts would actually qualify for the move-down. Put the yearly-default change on the page as a first-week action with its own expected churn effect.

strength: It is a tight, readable single recommendation. It has a break-even figure (about 1 in 3 Team 8+ customers moving down), an email that shows each customer's own bill next to the Agency price, and explicit go and stop thresholds. It also keeps the 12-month promise even if the test stops.
mistake: The base case assumes half of Essentials 8+ customers switch, which is optimistic. The yearly-billing signal is mostly ignored: yearly is offered only at the switch, and the default toggle is never fixed. The 15-channel cap leaves a cliff for the many 8+ accounts near it.
to10: Add a separate, cheap yearly-default change that ships to everyone. Show a range of cases with the break-even clearly flagged. Test the cap by checking how many 8+ accounts sit above 15 channels. Close the gap between the go and stop thresholds.

strength: Complete 24-post grid plus six warm drafts using the customers' own phrases (day three, replaying emails, parked before pickup). The stop list is clear, and the success table gives low and high projections with working shown.
mistake: Says no post needs review, yet draft 5 mentions work stress and draft 3 mentions replaying emails and sleep. It also adds a speculative live stream, and a few figures are shaky (24 posts with 16 clips is fine, but 'Awake at 2am' in week 3 would trigger insomnia review and isn't flagged). The 'review and then Tuesday 24 Nov' line is correct, but the plan never says when to submit later posts.
to10: Flag the later titles that need review (such as 'Awake at 2am') with a submit-by date of 16 Nov, drop the live-stream tangent, and tighten the word count. Make drafts 3 and 6 clearly narrator clips or sleep-led.

strength: Clear, tight structure: lead with sleep, narrator clips and evening posting. It handles review timing explicitly (batch submit on 16 Nov, live from 24 Nov) and sets realistic success thresholds, including a caution that the 5.9% rate came from only 5 posts.
mistake: Only one repeated weekly pattern with weekly angles but no post-by-post titles for weeks 2 to 4. It keeps stress-at-work carousels and a kindness-labelled parent clip. The review batch is declared before the content exists, and the 'every later post needs review' assumption is blunt. The drafts also use hashtags, which is fine, but 'Want to try?' repeats.
to10: Add a week-by-week list of topics for weeks 2 to 4 with a review flag on each. Label the parent clip as its own theme, and add a recut or best-performer rule to give the plan more range.

strength: The whole series is built around the two habits (recurring task and second device). It adds a branching email 5 that sends the missing habit, platform-specific email 3 versions, a control group and a guardrail, and it says what to do first.
mistake: The trigger logic is loose and partly unclear. Email 3 is sent '24 hours after first recurring task, or day 4', and email 5 depends on 'Did both' branches, which blur the one-tip, one-button rule. The 'no activity' email is also sent 'days 2 to 14'. The word count looks tight. Pro is dropped to after day 30, which is unspecified. The control group is 'no onboarding emails', which is risky. 'Each extra point is 1,800 people a quarter' is correct, but email 5 sends mixed content.
to10: Tighten the trigger rules so each email has one clear send rule. Make email 5 a single tip and button, or split it by platform cleanly. Give each email a clear 'worked if' number and state exactly when Pro goes out. Keep the control group gentler.

strength: Each email is clean and ready to send: trigger, subject, preview, body, button, goal and 'worked if' are all laid out. It follows one tip and one button, uses typed quoted examples, and branches email 3 by platform. The drop section is specific with numbers and ties to the parent and student customers.
mistake: Email 5 is a Pro upsell, which spends one of five slots on selling instead of the second habit. There is no email that goes after the missing habit. Email 3 is on a fixed day 3, so some users get it just after a day-2 email. Email 2's 'Skip if already recurring' leaves those users with no nudge toward the second habit. The Pro reminder claim is a feature assumption, and a few subject lines are close to the 45-character limit ('Let's Todoist remember the repeats' is 36, so fine).
to10: Replace the Pro email, or add a habit-gap email that sends the missing habit by platform. Add a stronger inactivity design. Add a note on desktop signups. State the Pro data and tie the Pro email to a number.

strength: It turns our own numbers into trials per 1,000 clicks and trials per page, then ranks each move by extra trials and extra paid customers. It also covers both buyers: a GA4 migration page for Maya and an agency page for Tomas.
mistake: The forecasts are optimistic. They assume /vs-google-analytics jumps to a 9% CTR in the top 3 and give a 175-trial ceiling. The cookie banner post is ranked low because it is valued at the blog conversion rate, even though it answers Maya's exact question and could be turned to point at the trial.
to10: Give a realistic range instead of a ceiling, put the near-page-one cookie pages first, add dates and owners, and provide ready-to-use titles for the first rewrites.

strength: It reads like a decision I can act on. It opens with a clear call, gives honest bad news about total clicks, and puts conservative ranges on every move. It sets real calendar dates, a title and meta written in our voice, a section-by-section outline for Monday, and rules for keeping or rolling back changes.
mistake: Six of the twelve writer slots go to refreshing existing vs pages. Those are mostly fact-and-date updates and could be lighter, which would free slots for more new pages for Maya's fears, such as moving from GA4. The cookie banner post is also bundled lower in the ranking than its intent deserves.
to10: Make the vs-page refreshes lighter and use the freed slots for a GA4 migration page and more new comparisons. Move the cookie banner and no-cookies pages up as the quickest wins.

strength: The segment pick is sharp, with correct seat math (0.73 paid seats per recruiting signup against 0.17 for the next best segment). The hero uses Priya's own 'email tennis' phrase. The deciding metric only counts recruiting teams that get a first booking within 7 days, so curious visitors don't skew the test.
mistake: Buttons swing between 'Get started' and 'Book a demo' on a page aimed at teams. Version B's headline reads awkwardly. The line 'that is your week gone' is an inflated claim that breaks our numbers-over-adjectives rule.
to10: Use 'Book a demo' consistently and offer 'Get started' as a secondary link. Tighten hero B. Put the security section right next to the demo form. Say how long the test needs to run for the traffic we get.

strength: It is close to shippable. It has a page title and meta description, a single consistent demo button with self-serve as the secondary option, and security moved up so it sits right before a 4-field demo form. The sample size (about 13,400 per version) and the seat projection both check out. Hero B uses Priya's 'skip whoever is on PTO' wording.
mistake: The sample-size calculation uses the 3.1% homepage signup rate as its baseline without saying that this is a different rate from 'qualified starts'. The hero uses the brand's 'back and forth' line and drops Priya's sharper 'email tennis'.
to10: State the baseline assumption behind the sample size. Fold 'email tennis' into section 2. Add a placeholder slot for a real recruiting customer quote once one exists.

strength: Honest and well organized. It has the three numbers, a correct runway range, a clean table of where the burn went, and three asks that each name a profile, an owner and a date.
mistake: Customer A comes second, behind the AI-builder story, and the asks sit at the very bottom. A phone reader who stops early learns neither. The '9 points of margin, more than the 7-point drop' aside is clever but could confuse investors.
to10: Put Customer A and a one-line summary of the asks in the first screen. Give the 48-hour fix a ship date. Add short blurbs angels can forward.

strength: Built for the lead partner on a phone. It gives the three numbers and the asks with dates in the first screen, then puts Customer A first in the bad news and notes it will show in February ARR. The margin fix has a ship date, and the asks come with blurbs angels can forward.
mistake: It states as settled that the VP role is now based in New York and that the fix ships by 27 November. Both are assumptions I would need to confirm before sending. The September runway of 52 months in the table may draw questions without context.
to10: Confirm the New York decision and the ship date. Give a rough estimate of the margin recovery from the 48-hour pause. Add a sentence on how Customer A's loss will affect NRR.

strength: It targets the right segment and the pricing-change trigger, keeps every step link-free, and asks low-friction one-word questions that sound like one finance person talking to another. It also gives a clean reply and meeting forecast: about 7% replies and about 55 meetings across the 1,900.
mistake: The 9-to-4-day proof is in step 1 and repeated in step 4, so the later steps have no new proof to add. It also leaves out practical send rules: no unsubscribe or footer, and no plan for handling replies.
to10: Move the proof out of step 1 into step 2. Add an opt-out footer and a short guide for handling replies. Add one timing insight tied to the finance calendar.

strength: It reads like it was written by someone who knows finance. It times sends around month-end close and allows one contact per company. It adds an opt-out footer, a guide for handling replies, an A/B test and a clearly labelled bolder test, and all of it is grounded in the pilot numbers.

strength: The post is ready to publish. Salary is in the first line, the hours and weekend rotation are stated plainly, the welcome to career changers is real, and a sample customer email is already written into the application form.

strength: It turns the data into practical details: a local-hours table including Sydney's summer shift, about 8 or 9 rotation weekends a year, a projected reviewer-hours table, set interview questions, and an idea to keep a pool of strong past applicants.

strength: The numbers are worked and checkable: agencies are 60% of Semrush losses, Lite usage-limit exits are 32% of all churn, and multi-site accounts are 42% of free conversions. It also adds a bold, well-tied move 5 that puts a free Monday report inside Webmaster Tools as an agency hook.

to10: Add an 'as of' date. Give the data section more room so a grade-9 reader can follow it. Make move 1's target and projection agree. Say more clearly why the Lite fix is the fastest money, even if the agency report stays at #1.

strength: The story is clear: where we lose, where we don't, and our biggest leak isn't Semrush. Every claim is dated, and there's a neat retention insight (only 37% of a Lite group is left after 12 months). strength: A tight, dated plan with an owner on every task. It ranks channels by retained users with the math, builds the timeline around the 1 December freeze (authors get the build 17 November), and adds measurable targets plus a concrete plan B.

strength: Very strong launch gates: 1,000 real power-user beta setups with zero loss, a one-step undo, the top 200 extensions tested, a check that every claim is in the build, and a staged rollout tied to ticket limits. It takes our 'don't break my hotkeys' fear seriously.
mistake: Creators only get the build on 24 November, about two weeks before launch, which is tight for good videos. The X thread and email are full of placeholders, including a blank speed number. Most timeline rows lack owners, and a few tasks (300 staff setups, engineers on support) stretch a small team.
to10: Send creators the build a week earlier. Put an owner on every timeline row. Fill in or cut the placeholders so the drafts are postable. Add a plan B for when tickets or installs miss target.

strength: A tight, well-argued Agency plan. The revenue math checks out ($249k at risk, a $24.6k uplift, $76.53 average per Agency account), it names the Team move-down breakeven point, and the customer email sounds like us, including 'you can switch back.'

to10: Ship a yearly-by-default or in-app yearly offer alongside Agency. Explain the grandfathering timing for the board. Judge the test on net revenue per account, not only on switch rates.

strength: It catches all three things in my data: the 8+ churn leak, the hidden yearly option, and the 12-month promise limiting what can show up in two quarters. It also gives correct math across three cases, an honest check on whether yearly billing pays off in six months, and a sharp stop rule built on MRR per account.

strength: A tight, data-led case for sleep, narrator clips and evening posting, with correct installs-per-post figures, clear success targets and a mid-point check after week 2.
mistake: It sends weeks 2 to 4 for review without saying what those posts are, beyond one-line themes. Its own timing (live from Tuesday 24 November) also clashes with the Monday 23 November post in week 2.
to10: Add a post-by-post topic list for weeks 2 to 4 and fix the review-date clash. Work in the 'switch my brain off' hook, and our 'Take a breath. You've got this.' line, directly.

strength: A full 24-post calendar with an owner for each post and production deadlines. Drafts are in our real voice ('Take a breath. You've got this.'), each ends with one small action, and the targets have low and high cases tied to clear decisions.
mistake: Some week 3 and 4 hooks, such as 'Awake at 2am', come close to naming sleep problems without a review flag. Pausing text-on-screen video entirely is asserted more than argued.
to10: Mark which future posts might trigger clinical review and when to submit them. Trim to the word limit, and use the 'switch my brain off' line as a hook.

strength: The whole series serves the two habits that predict retention. Email 5 targets whichever habit each user is still missing, the skip and trigger logic uses only events our tool supports, and the mobile and web branches point each group to the right second device.

strength: Clean, very readable emails in our calm voice with good typed examples. The drop section ties back to our personas well, using the 'perfect on Sunday, gone by Wednesday' line, and the Pro email for engaged users is a sensible way to keep revenue in.
mistake: It spends the fifth slot on a Pro pitch instead of a second push toward the missing habit, so anyone who gets only one habit is never nudged toward the 67% 'both' group. It also claims timed reminders are Pro-only, and that needs checking.
to10: Replace or branch email 5 so users missing a habit get that habit, and send Pro only to those who have both. Email 3 should also be triggered after the recurring task rather than sent on a fixed day 3.

strength: The numbers check out (13% total click drop, 1,316 trials, 46 trials per vs page against 0.7 per post). The forecasts are cautious ranges tied to my own CTRs and conversion rates. Week 1 is a day-by-day list with a ready title, meta and page outline in our voice.

strength: The trials-per-1,000-clicks table makes the case plainly. The stop list includes merging or redirecting dead posts. The plan covers both Maya's fear of losing GA4 history and Tomas's DPO need.

strength: Complete and usable page. Segment choice backed by clear seat math (733 seats per 1,000 signups vs 12 for coaching). The page puts security and routing up where Priya needs them, and the A/B plan has a sample size and a clear decision rule.

PTO is skipped', and 'Send this to your security team'. The projection of 150 to 460 extra seats is speculative. The 'Monday' hook is used, but 'email tennis' is not. strength: The hero uses Priya's own words ('No email tennis'), the segment math is crisp (0.73 seats per signup vs 0.17 for sales demos), and unknowns are honestly marked in [brackets] instead of made up. The metric is well argued, tied to real use rather than clicks.

strength: Gives the three numbers first, with runway as a 33 to 37 month range. Ties the margin drop to AI-builder traffic and states the cost per revenue dollar (about 9 points). Ask 3 goes to the lead partner for help on pricing partner traffic.

It also carries two tables (burn drivers and a full glance table), which is heavier than the small table I asked for, and the asks have no forwardable text. The '9 points, more than the 7-point drop' line is confusing.

strength: The first screen has the three numbers, the quoted forecast miss and a one-line summary of the asks. Customer A is the first bad-news item, with the date and a note that the loss shows in February ARR. It uses my voice line, 'Here's what went wrong and what we're doing about it'. Each ask has a profile and a date, and two come with forwardable blurbs.
mistake: States 'The role is now based in New York' as settled when it is only an assumption. The Sept 52-month runway row looks alarming without context. It does not say Customer A's exit will lower NRR.
to10: Flag the New York decision more clearly. Add a line on Customer A's expected effect on NRR and runway. Trim the table so it is smaller, and explain why runway fell from 52 to 33 months.

strength: It opens on the decision (Controllers after a pricing change) and gives usable send rules: a monthly timing window, an opt-out footer and reply handling. The emails sound like a finance peer, use contractions and stay under 120 words. The 9-to-4-day proof appears as a plain sentence, with no link in step 1.

to10: Cut it to 900 words and drop the 'bolder move'. Give step 1 a lighter ask than a call. Keep one clean ask in step 4. Quote the expected reply rate once, with the pilot caveat.

strength: The reply-rate section is the most honest of the two. It plans on about 7%, calls 6.8% the floor, and refuses to multiply the segment and trigger gains because the pilot never tested them together. It also loads contacts weekly as flags fire, which uses the data tool the way I would.

'A lot of controllers tell me' invents conversations the sender never had. The emails also have no opt-out line or address, and the tone is stiffer because it avoids contractions.
to10: Make the asks only what we can deliver, such as a reply and a short call. Remove the invented 'controllers tell me' and the unsupported product claim. Add the opt-out footer, use contractions, and get under 900 words.

strength: Covers every data signal: APAC hours with a local-time table, weekend rotation stated near the top, the reply exercise as the application, a transparent reviewer-hours estimate, and a bolder talent-pool idea, all in a post that sounds like us.
mistake: The scorecard weights interview-stage items at 45% even though interview impression correlated only 0.11. The writing weight is 55%, but the process is heavy. It also says 'two of the three recent hires who left' when it was 3 of 9 hires with 2 citing the rotation. The assumptions and the post are crowded, and the word count likely goes over 1,100.
to10: Weight writing higher, shrink the interview share, tighten to the word limit, fix the leaver wording, and make the post's opening less dense so the hard parts read calmer.

strength: Clean, calm post with salary first, honest hard parts, a concrete sample customer email in the form, and a scorecard that puts 50% on writing and says plainly why, with 1/3/5 for each line.
mistake: Adds a longer written exercise and a 'why this job' essay, which adds work for applicants and a little to reviewers. Also gives only a Singapore/Manila/Perth time conversion, and the 4-day-week dates are loosely placed.
to10: Add a time-zone table for Tokyo and Sydney, drop the 'why this job' question, and give the timeline of the later steps (exercise and calls) in the post.

strength: The 'where we lose / where we don't' sections are built from checked numbers, such as 13 of 100 trials lost to Semrush from agencies and Lite producing 70% of churn. It also says plainly what not to build (PPC parity, solo price cuts).
mistake: It invents a date ('Data as of November 2026'), which our own rule against undated sources should rule out. Move 1's first step is 40 interviews rather than shipping something, and Move 5 (link-data studies) is generic content advice with weak numbers behind it.
to10: Remove the made-up date. Make Move 1's first step a concrete beta rather than research. Replace the content-marketing move with something tied to the data, and put the Lite limit fix first or flag it clearly as the fastest money.

strength: An up-front answer with win/tie/lose, 'do first', 'stop' and 'don't spend on' lines gives me the decision in one read. Every move has an owner, a first step and a success metric, and the projections check out. The 'Here's the data' heading sounds like us.
mistake: Move 5 (a free report inside Webmaster Tools) is a bold bet that could undercut paid reporting, and it is only partly de-risked. The Lite limit fix could rank higher as the cheapest win.
to10: Rank the Lite top-up first or flag it as the quickest money. Give Move 5 a clearer test and cost estimate, and add an owner-ready success threshold for Move 4.

strength: A dated calendar with owners that fits the small team and the 1 December freeze. It makes the author build go out on 17 Nov so bugs surface before the freeze, and it has a six-point go/no-go gate on carry-over. The retained-user math is right (17,080 total) and it has targets and a plan B.

to10: Rank strictly by users kept, or explain why the order differs. Trim to the word limit. Name a few real authors in the X post and email. Add an in-app message for the update, and say how support gets staffed beyond the rota.

strength: The gates are thorough: a 1,000-user beta on real setups, a one-step undo, a staged rollout, and engineers on support shifts during the freeze. Each one speaks to the 'don't break my hotkeys' fear and the 58% ticket problem.
mistake: The drafts are not ready to post. The X thread has blank placeholders in the speed post, and the author names and support address are bracketed. The calendar has no named owners and there are no success targets. Some gates, such as undo and testing the top 200 extensions, are invented asks that engineering may not be able to meet before the freeze.
to10: Fill in the drafts so they can go out as written. Add owners and measurable targets. Rank channels strictly by users kept. Make the gates match what engineering can deliver before 1 December. Give the X launch a single clean post.

strength: One clean recommendation, a $79 Agency plan, with revenue math that ties out to my numbers. It includes a break-even on Team move-downs, a customer email that shows each person's own current bill, and clear go and stop rules.

to10: Add a proper yearly-billing step, a faster win than the new plan. State plainly that the first two quarters come from churn reduction because of the 12-month price hold. Support the 50% switch and 5% churn assumptions with something firmer.

strength: It uses all three signals in my data: the Essentials 8+ leak (374 customers, $23.9k a month), the yearly-billing gap, and the 12-month promise. It gives low, mid and high cases and says honestly that the low case is near zero and yearly won't help within two quarters. It has a dated plan and a measurable stop rule.
mistake: $99 is about 55% above what an 11-channel Essentials customer pays now, so the 25% upgrade assumption looks optimistic. The 'bolder move' section edges toward a menu when I asked for one recommendation. It is dense and uses terms like MRR and holdout.
to10: Price Agency closer to the current bill, or defend $99 with evidence. Drop or fold in the bolder-move section. Write in plainer words and keep a single recommendation, with the yearly change clearly secondary.

strength: The numbers are checked and correct (450 vs 95 installs, 6,580 projection, 3.4% save rate). The plan is clear about review timing, the stop list is complete, and week 1 needs no review. The success targets include a check after week 2.

It also sends all of weeks 2 to 4 for review as a batch, though they are not drafted and the wording could avoid review. Wednesday at 14:30 and a Tuesday kindness carousel dilute the evening focus.

strength: It gives a full 24-post calendar with owners and production deadlines. The drafts use customer phrases ('brain still on', 'replaying emails', 'quit by day three') in our warm voice, with 'Take a breath. You've got this.' and a small action at the end. Four of the six posts are narrator clips, nearly all in the evening, and the success table has high and low cases.
mistake: It says none of the 24 posts need review, but titles like 'Awake at 2am' edge toward a condition. The 'photo carousel' conflicts with our illustrated look. The optional live-stream idea is outside the brief and adds risk.
to10: Flag any later post that might need review and say when to submit it. Keep the carousels illustrated, not photo. Drop or shrink the live-stream idea. Trim the length so it clearly stays within 1,200 words.

strength: The whole series is built on the two habits (typed recurring task, second device), with a skip-if table, platform-split email 3, a calm inactivity email, and a catch-up email 5 that targets whichever habit is missing. It also drops the team invite and shortcuts emails with the numbers.
mistake: Success measures are grouped at the end, not given per email. The control group gets no onboarding emails at all, which is harsh. Email 5 has branching variants that are a little fiddly to read.
to10: Put a 'worked if' line under each email, use a softer holdout (the old series, not nothing), and simplify the email 5 variants into clear labeled versions.

strength: Each email has a clean trigger, subject, preview, body, button, goal and 'worked if' line, which matches my brief exactly. The drop section is well argued and mentions parents and students.
mistake: Email 5 is a Pro upsell, so only two of five emails teach the habits that drive retention. Email 3 goes out on a fixed day 3 instead of reacting to what the user did, and nothing catches people who skip a habit.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a habit catch-up email keyed to the missing habit, and trigger email 3 off the earlier events instead of a fixed day.

strength: Every number checks out. That includes the 13% total drop, 46 trials per comparison page against under 1 per post, ranged trial projections tied to each group's real conversion rate, and the 38% paid maths. It is built on real calendar dates and uses exactly 12 writer slots and 3 developer days.

Old decaying posts are left live and unchanged instead of being merged or redirected into the pages that convert. It also spends six slots refreshing vs pages and adds no GA4-migration page for Maya's main fear.
to10: Retitle the cookie banner post and /privacy-focused-web-analytics in Week 1. Add a consolidate-or-redirect step for dead blog posts. Swap one vs refresh for a 'keep your GA4 history' page.

strength: The diagnosis table is clean and gives trials per 1,000 clicks and per page. The stop list includes merging or redirecting dead posts. It covers both buyers' blockers, with a GA4-migration page for Maya and a DPO-ready agency page for Tomas, all inside 12 pages.
mistake: The forecast shows only best-case ceilings, such as reaching the top 3 for 'google analytics alternative' and 175 trials a month, with no range. It also claims Fathom offers self-hosting, which is risky on a page meant to be fair and factual. Month 3 depends on an audit by a 'strategist' we don't have, and weekly trial reporting will be noisy.
to10: Give low and high ranges instead of ceilings and fact-check the competitor claims. Name an owner for the blog audit. Put dates on the plan and write out the actual title and meta for Monday.

strength: The segment math is right: about 1,540 of 2,717 paid seats, and 0.73 paid seats per recruiting signup against 0.17 for the next best segment. The hero uses Priya's own words, 'No email tennis.' Brackets clearly flag every fact we still need to supply.
mistake: Security sits in section 6, three sections before the demo form, so the blocker isn't answered where Priya decides. Section 2 also says 'three or four emails' and 'your week gone' without support, which is an adjective claim, not a number. The buttons switch between Get started and Book a demo, which dilutes the team ask.
to10: Move security right next to the demo form. Cut the unsupported email-count claim. Keep the buttons on Book a demo. Size the test in visitors.

strength: The order is exactly right: hero, booking, round robin, routing, reminders, tools, then security immediately before a 4-field demo form. The numbers check out: 733 against 12 seats per 1,000 signups, about 13.4k visitors per arm for a 20% lift, and 150 to 460 projected paid seats. mistake: The hero uses our house line 'without the back and forth' instead of Priya's sharper 'email tennis.' The sample size uses the 3.1% homepage signup rate as a stand-in for the new metric without saying so. At this length it likely runs close to or over the 1,000-word limit.
to10: Bring 'email tennis' into the H1 or Version B. State that the 3.1% baseline is a proxy. Trim the meta and projection extras to stay safely under 1,000 words.

strength: The margin math is tight. It works out that the $0.9M compute rise is about 9 points on roughly $10.4M of monthly revenue, which covers the 7-point drop. It also shows direct databases grew only 2.6%. The burn table and the 33–37 month runway range are both correct.

to10: Put Customer A and a one-line summary of the asks right under the three numbers. Name the effect on NRR and on February ARR. Commit to the New York base instead of floating it. Add short intro text investors can forward.

strength: Built for a partner reading on a phone. The preview line flags the lost customer, the three numbers come first, and the asks with dates follow right after. Customer A leads the bad news, with the February ARR impact stated. The asks are specific and include intro text ready to forward. The runway row is correct for both months (52 to 33).
mistake: It states two things as done that are really assumptions: the New York relocation and a 27 November ship date. It also likely runs a little over 700 words. It never says that losing Customer A will pull NRR down.
to10: Trim to under 700 words. Add a line on the expected NRR impact and the expected margin recovery from the 48-hour pause, given as a range. Confirm the New York decision and the ship date before sending.

strength: Tight, on-brand emails built on the right segment, the pricing trigger and the rev rec rebuild pain, with no links. It adds practical extras: reply handling, an opt-out footer and an A/B test.
mistake: The 12th-to-15th start window can hold a fresh pricing flag for up to a month, which works against the weekly trigger. It also says 'leave out about 4,100' while only loading flagged contacts, so the real load size is never stated.
to10: Send within days of each weekly flag instead of on a fixed monthly window. State how many flagged Controllers we can realistically expect per week, and turn that into a meetings number.

strength: The expectations section is honest and fully worked out: it plans on 6.8%, deliberately does not multiply the two gains, and its 1,900-contact math checks out (about 130 replies, 65 positive, 55 meetings). It also gives a clear weekly load-on-flag rule.
mistake: Step 2 slips into a product pitch ('Chargebee is built so...'). It also leaves out pilot Controllers, who are not on the new list, and the full-1,900 projection quietly assumes every one of them gets a pricing flag.
to10: Cut the product line in step 2. Size the weekly flagged volume realistically rather than assuming all 1,900 fire. Add an opt-out footer and a plan for handling replies.

strength: Puts the Asia-Pacific hours and the weekend rotation at the very top of 'the hard parts', with an accurate local-time table that includes Sydney daylight saving and a correct 8 to 9 weekends a year. The reviewer-hours math also checks out: 94 to 129 hours against 160.

to10: Shift weight from interview rows to written evidence, for example a written handover note and the reply itself. Include the sample customer email in the post, and trim it to stay safely under 1,100 words.

strength: Follows our data directly. Writing to customers carries 50%, a handoff note is scored in writing, and conversation is held to 15%. A real, HEY-flavoured customer email sits right in the post, and it says plainly 'we're reading how you write, not whether you know the fix.' That last line is exactly what the career changer needs to hear. The math is correct: 4.6 minutes each last time, 70 hours now, about 7 hours for second reads.
