to10: Give timings for the later stages. Add two or three fixed interview questions. List more APAC cities, such as Tokyo and Sydney, with daylight-saving notes. Consider dropping the 'why this job' box, since it adds reading time for little signal.

strength: The numbers check out: 13.0 agency trials per 100 lost to Semrush, 60% of all Semrush losses, Lite at 70% of churners, 37% 12-month Lite retention, and 42% of AWT conversions from multi-site accounts. A clear 'what we should not do' section rules out PPC parity and creator discounts.
mistake: Move 1 invites PPC scope creep by pulling in clients' ad data. Its 19% headline gain assumes we win back a quarter of agency losses, which is optimistic and not backed. The 'November 2026' data date is made up, which breaks our dated-source rule.
to10: Make the Lite top-up the fastest-money move with explicit timing. Keep the report to data we already have. Tie the content study to a dated, real dataset. Size Move 1 more conservatively.

strength: The opening answer is built for an exec: lose / tie / win / not-Semrush, then what to do first, what to stop, and what not to fund, all with checked numbers. Move 1's beta uses only data we already have, and its sizing (5–10% more new paid customers) is cautious and correct.
mistake: Move 5 overlaps heavily with Moves 1 and 3 and takes the slot of a teach-first content move that suits our brand. Move 3 compares against the old 9.2% rate when the comparison should be the live holdout.
to10: Replace or fold in Move 5 so the five moves cover separate ground. Put the Lite top-up first as the quickest money. Add dates to the data periods.

strength: The numbers hold up and connect: retained users per channel, the 9-creator projection (6,980 to 9,240 kept), and 240 falling to about 100 tickets a day. They link straight to a calendar that gets author bug reports in before the 1 December freeze.
mistake: The table claims to rank by users who stay, but it puts extension authors (2,470) above X (3,740) and Hacker News above Product Hunt without saying why. The 'growth potential' logic is left unstated.
to10: Say plainly why authors outrank X despite fewer retained users. Name the specific authors or extensions credited in the X post. Make the staged update a firm gate rather than an optional 'bolder move'.

strength: Strong launch gates: a 1,000-user real-setup migration beta, one-step undo, a staged rollout tied to a ticket limit, a ban on claiming unshipped features, and a speed post held until a measured number exists. Engineers on the support rota during the freeze is a smart use of the team.
mistake: Creators only get the build on 24 November and the power-user beta starts 23 November, which leaves little time before the freeze. The drafts are full of placeholders. The email tells all 420,000 users to update now while the plan stages the rollout.
to10: Give creators the build in the week of 16 November. Fill in the author credits and the speed number. Line the email up with the staged rollout. Explain why authors are ranked above X.

strength: It goes after both real leaks. It targets the Essentials 8+ churn and ships a yearly-billing fix that needs no price change. The math checks out: $63.91 per account, 374 accounts and $23.9k lost a month, $2.21M total, and the $58.09 vs $60 yearly comparison. It also says plainly that the board's two-quarter window can't count on repricing existing customers.
mistake: At $99 the plan is a $35 jump from the typical $64 Essentials 8+ bill, which may hold down upgrades, and the low case is close to zero. The 'bolder move' section edges toward the menu I asked it to avoid. Some passages are number-dense and read above grade 8.
to10: Justify the $99 price point against a lower one, such as $79. Drop or shrink the bolder-move section. Simplify the revenue section for a plain reader. Add the customer's own current bill to the email.

strength: It fits our voice best. The email shows each customer their own bill next to the Agency price, with no deadlines and an option to switch back. The numbers are correct: $249k, 29% of churned revenue, $24.6k and $21.9k on day one. It also names the break-even point on Team move-downs, about 1 in 3.
mistake: The yearly-billing signal gets only a mention at the point of switch. It never fixes the monthly default on the pricing page or the missing in-app yearly offer, which is the cheapest and fastest win. It also leaves an unexplained gap between its 'go' thresholds and its 'stop' thresholds.
to10: Add a yearly-billing fix for everyone: show both prices side by side and offer yearly in-app. Close the gap between the go and stop criteria. Show a revenue range of cases tied to the board's two-quarter window.

strength: A full 24-post calendar with named hooks, plus a sharp opening that tells me the decision and the first deadlines for the editor and designer.
mistake: It dodges review instead of planning it. It never says to submit anything on 16 Nov, but week 3's 'Awake at 2am' sits close to insomnia territory and could easily get flagged.
to10: Batch-submit any borderline weeks 2 to 4 posts on 16 Nov with a clear review flag per post, and stop pasting the brand tagline into multiple captions.

strength: Practical review handling: submit weeks 2 to 4 as one batch on 16 Nov, live from 24 Nov, and allow 8 business days for any rewrite. It also adds a sensible check on narrator save rates, since the baseline comes from only 5 posts.
mistake: Weeks 2 to 4 get only one-line angles, not post-level hooks, so the team still has 18 posts to invent.
to10: Add a week-by-week title grid like the one in the other plan, and cut the hashtags in draft 1 so it reads as one clean voice.

strength: Every email has a complete body that sounds like us. Each has one tip, one button, typed examples in quotes and short subjects. The second-device email branches correctly by signup platform.
mistake: Email 5 spends a slot on Pro instead of pushing the missing habit. The second-device email goes out on a fixed day 3 instead of being chained to the recurring-task trigger, so the two-habit sequence is looser than it should be.
to10: Chain email 3 to the recurring-task trigger. Turn the last slot into a 'missing habit' email, or justify keeping Pro with numbers. Measure both habits by day 7 per platform.

strength: The whole series is built on the two habits. Triggers are chained with skip rules, and email 5 targets whichever habit the user is missing. There is a contingency plan if the mobile-to-web email underperforms, and the 1,800-people-per-point math is correct.
mistake: The control group gets no emails at all, so it tests emails against nothing rather than new against old. Pro is pushed out of the series with no revenue reasoning. The inactivity window 'days 2 to 14' doesn't match a 3-day trigger.
to10: Hold out a group on the old series, not on no emails. Fix the inactivity timing. Add a short line on what dropping Pro from onboarding means for upgrades.

strength: Very usable operating plan. It fits the 12-page and 3-dev-day limit, uses our conversion data, gives ranges instead of fantasy forecasts, and the week-one brief is ready for a writer.
mistake: It says to leave old posts live and unchanged, except the cookie-banner post. I would rather merge or redirect decaying posts into the pages that convert. It also starts with /vs-google-analytics when the cookie-banner and no-cookies pages are cheap wins sitting near page one.
to10: Move the cookie-banner rewrite and the no-cookies retitle into week one, add a small consolidation plan for weak blog posts, and remove or soften the rollback rule based on one-position movement after four weeks.

strength: The conversion math is clean and owner-focused: trials per 1,000 clicks, paid-customer impact, and a clear stop list. It also catches Maya's old-data blocker and Tomas's DPO need.
mistake: The month-by-month order does not fully follow its own ranking: the no-cookies page is ranked second but pushed to month two. The /vs-google-analytics forecast is also a ceiling, not something I would bank on in 90 days.
to10: Put the cookie-banner and no-cookies work into the first week, make the forecasts more conservative by showing likely and ceiling cases, and tighten the developer tasks so one dev day a month is unquestionably enough.

strength: It picks recruiting for the right reason, shows the seat math cleanly, moves round robin, routing and security up, and gives me a nearly usable page with real proof placements and no fake logos or quotes.
mistake: A few lines assume product details a little too freely, like video links going out automatically and PTO being known from the calendar, and the hero could use the customer's phrase 'email tennis' more directly.
to10: Tighten any product claims against what Cal.com definitely supports, make the security CTA a real button or clean section action, and sharpen the hero around Priya's exact pain language.

strength: The opening strategy is excellent: it chooses recruiting, proves it with paid-seat math, and the hero speaks directly to Priya with 'right interviewer' and 'No email tennis.'
mistake: It leaves too many placeholders and includes a few unsupported specifics, like text reminders, rescheduling from the same link, and 'three or four emails' per interview.
to10: Remove bracketed placeholders, replace unsupported product claims with verified ones, and make the CTA strategy more consistent for a team buying flow.

strength: It connects the AI app-builder database growth to the margin problem instead of treating database creation as a simple win, and it explains burn and runway correctly.
mistake: Customer A should be the first bad-news item, not second after the AI-builder issue; the note is also a little too analytical for a phone-first investor update.
to10: Put Customer A and the ARR forecast miss even higher, tighten the copy, move the asks closer to the top, and make the 48-hour pause expected impact more concrete.

strength: It leads with the three numbers, puts the customer loss and forecast miss where investors will see them, and gives specific dated asks that investors can act on.
mistake: It assumes the 48-hour fix ship date and that the VP Enterprise Sales role has already moved to New York; I would want to confirm those before sending.
to10: Confirm the assumed dates and New York decision, add one sentence on the expected NRR impact from Customer A, and quantify the target compute saving once engineering has a range.

strength: It follows the data: Controllers/Heads of Finance at 50-300 person SaaS companies, triggered by pricing-page changes, with no links and a realistic 6.8%-7.9% reply expectation.
mistake: The load math is a little loose: if only pricing-change accounts are loaded, more than 4,100 of the 6,000 may stay out at first. Step 1 also asks for both current close length and a 'yes' reply, which slightly muddies the ask.
to10: Tighten the CTA in step 1 to one clean reply path, move the proof to step 2 or 3, and separate 'eligible universe' from 'loaded this week' in the list math.

strength: It makes the right strategic call on segment, trigger, no-link sending, and gives useful operating rules for timing, testing, and handling replies.
mistake: The 'bolder move' suggests sending to untriggered watch-list Controllers, which cuts against the strongest signal in the pilot. The 'leaves out about 4,100' math is also not right if no-recent-pricing-change Controllers are excluded.
to10: Remove the watch-list experiment, fix the load math, soften the 20-minute meeting asks, and keep the sequence more tightly focused on the pricing-change pain rather than adding invented send-window logic.

strength: It turns the data into the right hiring design: APAC hours, weekend rotation up front, no years/tool requirements, and the written reply as the main signal.
mistake: It is a bit long and process-heavy, and the application section does not include the actual customer prompt we would put in the form.
to10: Trim it to the limit, add the exact customer email prompt, and tighten the hiring steps so the post and internal process are clearly separated.

strength: The post is plain, warm, and very close to publishable, with the salary, APAC need, weekend rotation, and no-experience-needed message handled well.
mistake: It adds a 'why this job' mini cover letter and a longer exercise after the application, which weakens the clean move toward using the written customer reply as the main filter.
to10: Remove the low-signal 'why this job' question, make the application reply the main written screen, add a little more structure to the interview scorecard, and state the full post-interview timing.

strength: It correctly separates the real Semrush problem from self-inflicted churn: agencies/reporting/PPC are the competitive gap, while Lite limits and plan cliffs are our fastest fix.
mistake: I would probably put the Lite limits/pricing fix first or make clearer that it is the fastest money, even if agency reporting is the bigger competitive bet.
to10: Rank the Lite fix first or explicitly split 'fastest cash' from 'biggest Semrush defense,' add a revenue-weighted view if available, and tighten the reporting move into a smaller MVP with exact report modules.

strength: Very clear, number-led diagnosis with the right core answer: agencies are the Semrush battleground, and Lite churn plus multi-site AWT onboarding are big underused levers.
mistake: Move 5 mostly duplicates moves 1 and 3, and the first reporting MVP built only from our existing SEO data may not answer the agency buyer's 'clients care about leads' problem strongly enough.
to10: Merge the two reporting ideas into one sharper agency reporting plan, connect it to analytics/conversion data rather than only Ahrefs data, and put the Lite usage-limit fix more clearly as the fastest payback move.

strength: It finds the right launch bet: creators and extension authors first, migration risk as the launch gate, Product Hunt/HN as secondary reach. It also gives usable launch copy in the right Raycast voice.
mistake: The channel ranking table says it is ranked by retained users, but puts extension authors above X despite fewer retained users in the 2025 data; it needs a clearer explanation that authors are prioritized for quality and upside, not raw retained count.
to10: Tighten the channel ranking so the math and priority order do not look contradictory, add one clearer support staffing rota, and make the staged rollout a firm recommendation if technically possible.

strength: It is strong on risk control: migration proof, restore path, staged rollout, support prep, tracking links, and beta testing with power users are all owner-level concerns.
mistake: It overreaches operationally: 1,000 real beta migrations with zero losses, a one-step restore, top 200 extension tests, and engineers joining support may not be feasible inside this small team and pre-freeze window. It also leaves too many placeholders in launch copy.
to10: Make the gates realistic for the team and dates, remove unsupported assumptions like engineers being free during code freeze, finish the copy without placeholders, and resolve the ranking contradiction between retained-user math and channel order.

strength: It picks the right leak: high-channel Essentials customers, and gives a simple flat plan with clear customer messaging and a real stop rule.
mistake: It underuses the yearly-billing signal; we know yearly is a major retention lever, but this only offers it at the Agency switch instead of fixing the pricing page and in-app billing flow.
to10: Add the yearly-billing change as part of the same recommendation, tighten the month-6 math explanation, and stress-test the 15-channel cap and Team cannibalization with clearer break-even numbers.

strength: It sees both big signals: the 8+ Essentials churn problem and the hidden yearly-billing retention lever, while respecting the 12-month price promise and the board’s two-quarter window.
mistake: The 25-channel cap may be too generous and could hide revenue loss from the highest-channel Essentials accounts; the average-account math may not catch that tail risk.
to10: Narrow or model the channel cap more carefully, remove the extra 'bolder move' so it stays as one recommendation, and show the Agency economics by channel count so we can see where upgrades become discounts.

strength: It makes the right strategic shift: sleep, evening posting, narrator clips, and fewer weak themes/formats. The 24-post table and six drafts are close to something the team could run.
mistake: The review timing note is a bit off, and the plan is slightly casual with riskier wording like 'expect fatigue' and a live-stream idea that is outside the core ask.
to10: Tighten the review guidance, remove the extra experimental live idea or clearly mark it as optional, and polish a few captions to feel a little more Headspace-soft.

strength: Very clear, warm, and on-brand. It reads like Headspace, uses the right data points, and the six drafts are easy to hand to the editor and designer.
mistake: The 4-week plan is less developed than it should be: it repeats the same weekly structure and only gives broad weekly angles, not a full post-by-post plan. The review timing also creates a possible gap for Monday 23 November.
to10: Add a true 24-post calendar with specific angles for each week, fix the review timing, and make the measurement plan tie more directly to each theme and format.

strength: It builds the whole series around the two retention signals that matter: recurring tasks and second-device sign-in, while keeping the copy calm, specific, and close to Todoist voice.
mistake: The Pro email is sensible, but it is less important than getting the remaining users to the second core habit; I would consider making email 5 a missing-habit email instead.
to10: Use the fifth email to dynamically push the one habit the user has not done yet, then move Pro fully out of onboarding or reserve it for a later monetization sequence.

strength: The strategy is sharp: focus only on the two behaviors that predict retention, branch by platform, and use email 5 to drive the missing habit instead of selling too early.
mistake: It is less finished as usable email copy, especially email 5, and a few operational assumptions are shaky, such as stopping the series once both habits are done and using a no-onboarding control group.
to10: Turn the dynamic logic into fully written variants, tighten the trigger plan to only what the tool can reliably do, and polish the copy so every email has one clear tip, one clear button, and no internal test notes mixed into the customer-facing work.

strength: It makes the right core call fast: stop general blog work, shift capacity to comparison and cookie-related pages, and gives a concrete week-one task list the writer can start on Monday.
mistake: It leaves too much upside on the table by prioritizing a /vs-google-analytics rewrite before the two no-page comparison terms, and one key statement is off: 46 trials per comparison page vs fewer than 1 per blog post overstates the blog gap because blog posts average about 0.7 trials per page.
to10: Tighten the projections and page-ordering, add the explicit consolidate/redirect plan for decaying blog posts, and make the first-week tasks start with the two cheap wins the data points to: the cookie banner post and the without-cookies page.

strength: It reads the data well, quantifies upside clearly, and gives a sensible month-by-month plan that stays mostly within capacity and keeps the brand constraints in view.
mistake: It adds too much that was not earned by the brief: the GA4 rewrite forecast is too aggressive, it introduces new pages that may not match proven search demand, and it says to send the draft to the owner even though the brief says the owner is not available.
to10: Cut the speculative pages, fix the over-optimistic traffic forecasts, and refocus the first 30 days on the highest-intent proven opportunities already in the data: missing comparison pages plus the two near-page-one cookie queries.

strength: It picks the right segment with the right seat math and structures the page around the real recruiting jobs to be done: stop email back and forth, spread interviews fairly, route candidates, then handle security.
mistake: It gets a little too expansive and drifts into strategy and test protocol beyond the copy brief, and the CTA pattern is less disciplined than the brand rule of one action per section.
to10: Tighten to the sharpest sections, keep one primary action more consistently, and make the page feel even more like Cal.com by trimming extra explanation and polishing a few lines.

strength: It is closest to something I would actually ship: right segment, strong math, good order, direct copy, security surfaced properly, and practical implementation details that help me act on it.
mistake: The test metric is slightly weaker than it could be because it counts recruiting signups without the first-booking quality filter, which could over-reward lower-intent starts.
to10: Use the stronger qualified-start definition tied to first booking, and sharpen one or two hero lines so the emotional hook lands as hard as the best parts of the page.

strength: It reads like our business, leads with the real bad news, and ties the margin drop to AI-builder traffic with the right fix and specific asks.
mistake: It adds a few owner-style notes that should not go to investors as written, especially the internal 'Assumptions in this draft' section and the slightly clunky line about margin points from monthly revenue.
to10: Remove the draft-only assumptions, tighten one or two sentences, and make the Customer A risk appear even earlier in the first problem block or headline summary.

strength: It is crisp, easy to scan on a phone, and has a strong investor-friendly structure with specific asks and clear ownership of the forecast miss.
mistake: It includes a wrong runway row in the table: September runway is shown as 52 months when $212.0M divided by $4.1M is about 51.7, and more importantly adding a runway change row is not that useful here; the date-specific shipping claim also feels made up rather than supported by the brief.
to10: Fix the numerical sloppiness, avoid unsupported exact dates, and add a bit more owner-level explanation of why AI-builder growth is low quality and what direct growth really looked like.

strength: It aims exactly at the winning segment and moment from the pilot, then turns the data into a focused sequence I could actually send.
mistake: A few asks are a bit too conditional or busy for the brand rule of one clean ask, and step 2 leans a little product-y.
to10: Tighten each CTA to one simple next step, keep every note even more peer-to-peer, and trim any line that sounds like selling instead of finance-to-finance.

strength: It still identifies the right audience and trigger, and it adds some practical operating rules around list hygiene and handling replies.
mistake: Several emails break the brief: step 1 and other steps mix more than one ask, promise a 20-minute call too early, and add rules not grounded in the data like send windows and compliance footer language.
to10: Strip it back to the tested signal, remove invented process rules, make each email one question and one ask, and align the tone more closely to our finance voice.

strength: It follows the data instead of HR habit: it centers writing, targets the overnight UTC gap with Asia-Pacific hours, and states the weekend rotation plainly near the top.
mistake: It adds extra process and assumptions I didn't ask for, especially the exact interview structure and some operational detail, while missing a concrete sample customer email in the application.
to10: Tighten it a bit, include the actual short customer reply prompt in the finished application, and simplify the process so it's immediately publishable without trimming.

strength: It sounds like us and is very usable right away: salary first, honest hard parts, career changers welcomed, and the application is much better than resumes plus cover letters.
mistake: It weakens the strongest signal by making the first-stage score mainly about writing tone, then adds a longer exercise later instead of using the best predictor earlier and more directly.
to10: Weight problem-solving inside the written exercise more heavily, make the scorecard more specific with 1/3/5 anchored to the actual work, and tighten the hiring flow around the proven signal instead of adding a second written stage.

strength: It identifies the real problem correctly: we lose to Semrush mainly in agencies because of reporting and PPC, while our biggest churn problem is self-inflicted on Lite, and it turns both into specific ranked moves with owners, first steps and success metrics.
mistake: Move 5 is a bit speculative and slightly overlaps with moves 1 and 3, so it is the least necessary item in an otherwise tight plan.
to10: It is already very close; the only improvement would be to tighten move 5 or replace it with a smoother plan-step fix for the in-house price jump so every move is more direct and less overlapping.

strength: It reads clearly, gets the main facts right, and correctly says not to chase PPC parity while prioritizing agency reporting, Lite limits, and the high-converting multi-site AWT segment.
mistake: It spends one of only five moves on generic content marketing instead of a more direct fix to the in-house price jump or plan/limit problem, so it is less focused on the fastest money in our own data.
to10: Replace the content move with a concrete packaging or pricing step for the Lite-to-Standard cliff and make the agency reporting move more execution-ready, with a tighter MVP and clearer success threshold.

strength: It reads the data the way an owner would: prioritises retained users over raw installs and makes migration reliability the main launch gate.
mistake: It labels X above Hacker News and Product Hunt in the ranking even though retained users are lower than Product Hunt, which creates a small inconsistency between the table and the stated principle.
to10: Tighten that channel ranking logic, remove a couple of speculative targets, and add slightly clearer owner assignments for each support and creator task.

strength: It understands that creators and extension authors should be the centre of the launch and gives a fuller staged rollout and audience plan than most generic launch checklists.
mistake: It adds major requirements and promises not grounded in the brief or team reality, like 1,000 beta users, restore functionality, engineering support shifts during freeze, and an under-8-hour reply target, so I would not trust it as an operating plan without reworking it.
to10: Keep the same structure but strip out invented capabilities, align the ranking and numbers more carefully to my data, and make every launch gate achievable with the actual team and timeline.

strength: It sees the core problem clearly: high-channel Essentials churn, not the small-business base, and it also notices that yearly billing is an underused retention lever constrained by the 12-month promise.
mistake: The revenue math and some claims around yearly are shakier than I would want before acting, and it drifts into a second recommendation at the end after saying to make one recommendation.
to10: Tighten the math, remove the extra 'bolder move,' and keep the recommendation strictly to one plan plus one simple yearly presentation change with cleaner board-window impact.

strength: It is easy to read, in our voice, and it squarely targets the right segment with a simple flat-price plan and clear customer communication.
mistake: The proposed price and package feel under-defended and the revenue math is less trustworthy; it also underplays the faster win from yearly uptake even though the brief and data point to it.
to10: Use more rigorous math, justify the price fence against Team cannibalization better, and include the honest yearly-billing change as part of the single recommendation because that is one of the few levers that can move results inside two quarters.

strength: It reads the business correctly: push sleep, narrator clips, and evening slots, while cutting low-value themes and formats. It also handles week 1 review timing sensibly and stays close to the brand voice.
mistake: It leaves one recurring parent post in a daytime slot without much evidence that the tradeoff beats the strong evening pattern, and the fixed weekly plan could be a little more explicitly tied to the best-performing themes every week.
to10: Make the weekly table even tighter around sleep-led evening posting, flag review status per draft more explicitly, and trim the weaker daytime test unless there is a clearer expected payoff.

strength: It clearly sees the main opportunity in sleep plus narrator clips, and the hooks feel on-brand and audience-aware.
mistake: It gets too loose with the facts and decision logic: saying sleep posts 'nearly triple' stress installs overstates the data, pausing text-on-screen video is not well supported, and introducing a TikTok live idea adds operational risk outside the brief.
to10: Keep the strong sleep-and-narrator strategy, but tighten every claim to the actual numbers, remove speculative extras like live streams, and make the plan more directly usable within the stated capacity and brief.

strength: It centers the whole series on the two behaviors most tied to retention and uses the actual trigger limits well, including platform branching and a calm inactivity nudge.
mistake: Email 5 is not fully written as a finished email body; it is more like conditional notes, and the 'control group' recommendation conflicts with judging the new series against the old one.
to10: Finish email 5 as clean final copy for each branch, tighten a couple of operational assumptions, and make the measurement plan consistent with an old-series holdout.

strength: It is very readable, on-brand, and the platform-specific second-device email is well judged for this audience.
mistake: It spends the fifth email on Pro instead of the missing retention habit, which misses the owner's main goal and leaves the strongest data signal underused.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a conditional final push to complete the missing habit, and fix the testing plan and unsubscribe guardrail to match the business context.

strength: It reads the data correctly: comparison pages are the trial engine, blog traffic is a distraction, and the plan fits the 12-page/3-dev-day capacity.
mistake: The forecast is a bit optimistic, especially assuming top-3 results for new comparison pages and a large jump for /vs-google-analytics within 90 days.
to10: Move the cookie banner and cookie-free analytics rewrites into week one, tighten the developer work to what fits in one day, and make the trial forecast more conservative with ranges.

strength: It is disciplined and usable: it ranks work by expected trials, uses capacity cleanly, gives the writer a real Monday-to-Friday start, and keeps the projections believable.
mistake: It is too passive on decaying blog posts and delays the cookie-free page to month two even though that query is a clear near-page-one opportunity.
to10: Put the cookie banner rewrite and /privacy-focused-web-analytics retitle into the first week, add a small consolidation plan for dead blog posts, and make sure the six comparison refreshes do not duplicate /vs-google-analytics.

strength: It picks recruiting for the right reason and shows the seat math clearly, then turns the data into a sensible page order with round robin, routing, and security moved up.
mistake: The hero is solid but a little less sharp than it could be; it says 'next free interviewer' more than 'right interviewer,' and a few extras like the projection and bolder move distract from the finished page.
to10: Tighten the hero around Priya’s exact pain, put security slightly closer to the main demo CTA, and remove or separate the extra testing/projection notes from the page copy.

strength: The hero and voice are very strong for Priya: 'right interviewer' and 'No email tennis' are clear, practical, and customer-led.
mistake: It includes a few unsupported or risky claims, like every interview taking three or four emails and text reminders, plus bracketed placeholders that make it less ready to hand straight to the team.
to10: Replace unsupported claims with the supplied data, remove placeholder quote/logo sections unless real assets exist, and make the final copy fully publishable without bracketed instructions.

strength: It gets the real story right: ARR growth missed the promise, margin fell because low-converting AI-builder traffic is creating compute cost, Customer A is leaving, and the VP Enterprise Sales hire is the key ask.
mistake: Customer A is not quite prominent enough; I would want that loss in the first screen alongside the margin issue, not second in the longer 'what went wrong' section.
to10: Move Customer A into the opening summary, tighten a few lines, and make the asks/assumptions feel less like draft notes after the signature.

strength: It is very usable for investors: three numbers first, bad news immediately, clear explanation of the margin problem, correct runway, and specific asks with dates and forwardable copy.
mistake: It asserts a few decisions and dates, like the 27 November ship date and the role now being New York-based, that I would want to confirm before sending.
to10: Confirm the assumed dates and New York decision, then send. Otherwise it already has the right order, tone, math, and asks.

strength: It picks the right segment and trigger, uses the pricing-change pain well, and gives a practical list plan with expected replies tied to the pilot data.
mistake: It adds a few extra rules and ideas that are not fully supported, especially the mid-month send window and the 'bolder move' to send untriggered contacts, which cuts against the strongest signal.
to10: Tighten the list math, remove the untriggered test suggestion, keep sends tied to the weekly pricing-change flag, and make the emails a little cleaner and less meeting-heavy.

strength: It follows the data almost exactly: Controllers/Heads of Finance, 50 to 300 person SaaS companies, recent pricing-page change, no links, and an honest expected reply range.
mistake: It slightly overstates confidence by saying the best segment plus best trigger should land at or above 7.9%, when the pilot did not test that exact combination.
to10: Make the reply forecast a touch more conservative, clarify that only the flagged subset of the 1,900 should be loaded now, and possibly move the 9-to-4 proof out of step 1 into a later email.

strength: It turns the data into the right hiring system: APAC hours, weekend rotation up front, no experience gate, and a short written customer reply as the first filter.
mistake: The interview stage is a little thin; it says two video conversations but does not give the team much structure for those conversations beyond the scorecard row.
to10: Add the exact interview questions, tighten a few lines for publication, and decide whether we truly want no resume at all or just no cover letter.

strength: The job post is warm, plain, and honest, with the hard parts, salary, remote setup, APAC hours, and weekend rotation all easy to see.
mistake: The application is not quite finished because it does not include the actual customer email applicants will answer, and too much of the scorecard weight still sits in interviews rather than written work.
to10: Include the exact written exercise in the post, move more signal into the written stage, add a handoff-writing task, and make the scoring less interview-heavy.

strength: It finds the real shape of the problem: Semrush is mainly an agency/reporting/PPC issue, while our biggest controllable leak is Lite limits and pricing friction. The math is useful and mostly right.
mistake: The fifth move, link-data content, is weaker and more generic than the first four; it feels less like a ranked competitive response and more like evergreen marketing.
to10: Tighten move 5 into a sharper retention or agency-sales move, and be a little clearer that the Lite limits test is the fastest cash win even if agency reporting is the bigger competitive bet.

strength: Very clear, blunt, and data-led. It explains the losses per 100 trials, the Lite churn math, and the multi-site AWT opportunity in a way a team could act on tomorrow.

to10: Separate the fifth move from the reporting/onboarding work or cut it, and make the Lite top-up/limits experiment one of the immediate actions alongside the agency reporting beta.

strength: It turns the migration/support failure into clear launch gates, support prep, staged rollout, and messaging that directly reassures power users.
mistake: The channel ranking is not fully consistent with its own retained-user math, and it assumes engineers can join support during freeze without checking capacity.
to10: Fix the retained-user ranking/priority explanation, tighten the timeline owners, and replace placeholders with final measured speed claims and named extensions/authors.

strength: It makes the right strategic call fast: community and creators first, migration as the launch blocker, Product Hunt/HN as secondary reach, with targets and plan B.

to10: Add a slightly more detailed launch-day sequence and support staffing rota, plus final author names/clips, while clarifying the channel ranking math.

strength: It finds the real leak, respects the 12-month price promise, adds a flat freelancer path, and also catches the under-used yearly billing lever that can help retention fast without a price rise.

strength: It is clean, focused, customer-friendly, and targets the right group with a flat plan and approvals without touching small-business pricing.
mistake: It largely misses the bigger yearly-billing opportunity: only 19% pay yearly, yearly churn is far lower, and we currently default to monthly and never re-offer yearly after signup.
to10: Add the honest yearly-billing change as part of the recommendation, show the two-quarter cumulative revenue impact more clearly, and make the test measure net MRR per account against a holdout, not just upgrade and downgrade rates.

strength: It puts the right things first: sleep, narrator audio, evening posting, and cutting weak app news/quote/focus content. The six drafts sound warm, simple, and very close to Headspace.
mistake: The review timing is a little over-cautious and the plan gives weekly angles rather than a fuller 24-post topic map, so the team would still need to fill in some later posts.
to10: Add a simple 24-post topic list for weeks 2 to 4 and tighten the review note to match the exact earliest go-live date.

strength: It gives the team a very usable 24-post map and correctly builds the plan around narrator clips, sleep, evening posting, and individual tracking.
mistake: It is a bit less disciplined: the 'sleep posts nearly triple' line is off, the live-stream idea adds distraction and risk, and some wording feels blunter than our warm Headspace voice.
to10: Remove the bolder live-stream test, soften the brand voice, clean up the few data/review details, and make sleep/evening the unmistakable priority throughout.

strength: It builds the whole series around the two strongest retention habits: recurring tasks and a second device, with good platform branching and a calm inactivity email.
mistake: Email 5 is a little complex and the assumptions around skipping/branching and button destinations need tightening before build.
to10: Make the branching rules fully build-ready, add a clear worked-if metric under each email, and simplify Email 5 into cleaner versions for each missing habit.

strength: The emails are very readable, on-brand, and mostly focused on the right early behaviors with clear goals and measures.
mistake: It keeps a Pro email inside onboarding at day 14 instead of using the fifth email to drive the missing retention habit, which weakens the main strategy.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a personalized missing-habit email, keep monetization out until users are active, and use the fifth slot to push recurring task plus second device completion.

strength: It makes the hard call I wanted: stop general blog output and move nearly all effort to comparison pages and the two high-impression 'no cookies' topics, with a concrete first week the writer can actually start on Monday.
mistake: It leaves too much value on the table by saying to leave most decaying blog posts unchanged, and some projections are a bit loose or optimistic, especially the docs and /privacy-focused-web-analytics assumptions.
to10: Tighten the forecasts, make the assumptions on /privacy-focused-web-analytics explicit with a safer range, and add a simple rule for consolidating weak blog posts into converting pages instead of mostly leaving them alone.

strength: It reads the data correctly at a high level, gives a fuller content system around buyer objections, and includes a sensible stop list with consolidation of dead posts.
mistake: It overreaches capacity and certainty in places: the /vs-google-analytics upside is overstated, it adds new pages without enough proof of search demand, and it tells the writer to send a draft to the owner even though the brief says the owner is unavailable.
to10: Cut the plan back to the highest-probability pages from the data, fix the forecasts, remove steps that depend on owner input, and make every month fit the exact 4-page/1-dev-day constraint more tightly.

strength: It picks recruiting for the right reason and proves it with seat economics, then structures the page around Priya's real pains: email back and forth, fair distribution, routing, and security.
mistake: It adds a few assumptions and placeholders that would need cleanup before publishing, and the CTA pattern shifts a bit between self-serve and demo without a single firm path for this segment.
to10: Tighten the page to one primary conversion path for recruiting teams, replace placeholders with real proof, and trim a little so it is closer to publish-ready without edits.

strength: It not only picks the right segment and messaging, but also surfaces practical CRO moves an owner can act on immediately, like moving security up, simplifying the demo form, and defining a concrete test and traffic requirement.
mistake: A couple of lines lean more into optimization commentary than finished page copy, and the qualified-start metric is slightly less tied to downstream quality than the stronger first-booking framing in the other draft.
to10: Keep the same strategy but simplify the decision metric to the clearest quality proxy, and remove a little of the testing commentary so the deliverable feels more like final copy than copy plus notes.

strength: It reads like it understands the real story in the numbers: the AI app-builder growth is hurting margin, Customer A is material bad news, and the VP Enterprise Sales hire is the key ask.
mistake: It includes an extra assumptions section and a few internal-style notes that make it feel slightly less like a finished investor email.
to10: Tighten the ending, remove the assumptions block, and make the first screen even cleaner by putting Customer A alongside the forecast miss immediately under the three headline numbers.

strength: It is very well prioritized for an investor reading on a phone: the miss, the margin drop, the customer loss, and the asks are all easy to find.
mistake: The runway row in the table is wrong for September and creates an avoidable factual error, which is a big trust problem in an investor update.
to10: Fix the runway math, keep only defensible calculations, and slightly sharpen the asks so each one is tied even more directly to the highest-priority problems.

strength: It aims squarely at the right segment and moment, uses the pricing-change trigger well, and turns the pilot data into clear list rules and a workable sequence.
mistake: Step 1 includes the 9-to-4 proof even though the brief strongly points to holding proof for a later step, and a few list/math details are a bit shaky or overreaching.
to10: Tighten the numbers and exclusions, move the proof out of step 1, and make the expected reply rate a bit more conservative and explicitly tied to tested conditions only.

strength: It is very well targeted, explains the logic cleanly, stays close to the pilot data, and gives practical loading rules and realistic expectations I could act on.
mistake: Some asks are a bit too gimmicky for a peer-to-peer finance voice (reply 'yes', 'steps', 'now' or 'later'), and it also puts proof into step 1 instead of saving it for later.
to10: Make the CTAs sound more natural for finance leaders, move the proof to a later step, and keep every assumption tightly bounded to what the pilot actually proved.

strength: It is tightly built around our actual data: it centers writing, targets the overnight UTC gap, and makes the weekend rotation impossible to miss.
mistake: It changes the role from the brief’s recruitment marketing specialist to a customer support specialist and adds a few process assumptions that may be more detailed than we need.
to10: Keep this structure and tone, but correct the role/title mismatch, trim a little, and make the scorecard math simpler and fully consistent.

strength: It sounds like us, welcomes career changers, and clearly explains a smarter application flow that should cut review time.
mistake: It adds a second written stage and a 'why this job' question without much evidence from our data, which weakens the owner’s goal of using the strongest signal early and keeping the process lean.
to10: Make the application even more evidence-led by relying mainly on the customer reply, tighten the scorecard with clearer 1/3/5 anchors for each stage, and remove extra steps that do not tie back to the hiring data.

strength: It isolates the real competitive problem to agencies, ties it to reporting rather than broad PPC parity, and also spots the bigger self-inflicted churn problem on Lite with numbers.
mistake: It says 'we lose to Semrush in one place' a bit too absolutely, then adds a fifth move that overlaps heavily with moves 1 and 3 instead of giving a more distinct final priority.
to10: Tighten the opening claim, remove or merge the overlapping fifth move, and make the success metrics a bit more realistic and directly attributable to each test.

strength: It is clear, numerate, and correctly identifies that agencies are where Semrush wins while Lite churn is the fastest non-competitive fix.
mistake: It adds a content-marketing move that is not one of the owner's main problems and weakens the focus; it also proposes joining client reports with ad and analytics data without support that this is the right first build.
to10: Stay tightly focused on the agency reporting gap, Lite limits, and multi-site AWT pipeline; replace the content move with a sharper agency or pricing action and keep first steps narrower.

strength: It uses our actual data to make the key call: prioritize creators and extension authors for retained users, and make migration reliability the main launch gate.
mistake: The channel ranking table is ordered by retained users except it places X above extension authors despite lower retained users, which muddies an otherwise strong point.
to10: Fix the ranking inconsistency, tighten a few projections, and add slightly more explicit staffing for support coverage during launch week.

strength: It sees the right strategic themes: retained users matter more than raw installs, migration is the big risk, and staged rollout plus early access for authors and creators are smart.
mistake: It introduces unsupported requirements and claims—like 1,000 beta users, top 200 extensions tested, an undo feature, engineers joining support, and a 6,750 retained-user creator projection—that are not grounded in the brief and may not be feasible for our team.
to10: Anchor every gate and forecast in our real constraints and data, remove made-up operational commitments, and tighten the launch-day messaging into one polished X post instead of a loose multi-post thread.

strength: It picks one clear move that targets the real problem in the data, and it correctly sees that the fastest two-quarter win must come from reducing churn and surfacing yearly billing rather than repricing the whole base.
mistake: The revenue math and framing get a bit loose in places: some figures are slightly off or insufficiently explained, and it adds a second 'bolder move' after saying there should be one recommendation.
to10: Tighten every number, keep to one recommendation only, and make the test and stop rule even cleaner by centering the decision on Essentials 8+ retention and Team cannibalization with no extra side proposal.

strength: It is easy to read, sounds close to our brand, and stays focused on the highest-value segment problem: high-channel Essentials customers who hate per-channel creep and need approvals.
mistake: It misses the bigger yearly-billing opportunity as part of the main recommendation and makes some assumptions and revenue claims that are too shaky for me to act on confidently, especially the price point and the month-6 math.
to10: Use our data more fully by combining the flat plan with an honest yearly push, show more defensible math, and prove the proposed price and channel cap are the right tradeoff against Team downgrade risk.

strength: It clearly leans into the strongest signals in the data: sleep, evening posting and narrator clips, and it gives a full 4-week schedule plus usable drafts.
mistake: It gets overconfident and sloppy in places: it says no posts need review, invents a fatigue risk without evidence, includes a weak Tuesday afternoon slot, and adds a live-stream idea outside the brief and capacity logic.
to10: Tighten the plan to the brief, avoid unsupported claims, handle review timing more carefully, and make week 1 and the channel/time mix cleaner and more defensible.

strength: It reads like someone understood the business fast: strong prioritization around sleep, narrator clips and evening posting, with a simple plan I could actually run.
mistake: It says to send weeks 2 to 4 for review even though those posts don't appear to need review, and the projected share-rate math is not really supported by the provided data.
to10: Keep the same structure but remove unnecessary review steps, tighten the metrics to only what the data supports directly, and add a little more variety in concepts without drifting off strategy.

strength: It centers the whole series on the two behaviors that actually predict retention and uses the allowed triggers well, including platform branching and a calm inactivity email.
mistake: Email 5 is presented as one email with multiple conditional versions and ends up a bit messy; it also adds extra operational ideas that are useful but slightly crowd the core deliverable.
to10: Make the final email logic simpler and fully polished for direct handoff, with each branch written as clean production copy and a slightly tighter measurement plan.

strength: It is clean, on-brand, easy to read, and it clearly explains why recurring tasks and a second device matter.
mistake: It uses the fifth email for a Pro pitch instead of another push toward the two habits, which misses the strongest retention opportunity in the brief and data.
to10: Use all five emails to drive the two key habits first, with branching based on what the user has or has not done, and leave Pro for later or outside this onboarding series.

strength: It follows the money: comparison pages and core product pages get the work, general blog traffic gets cut, and the trial-rate math is clear.
mistake: It knows the cookie-banner and cookie-free pages are cheap wins, but still waits until Month 2 for /privacy-focused-web-analytics and spends Month 1 on two new comparison pages first.
to10: Move the cookie-banner rewrite and cookie-free retitle into Week 1, before new pages, and make the 90-day forecast more conservative by separating likely gains from best-case ceilings.

strength: It is disciplined and usable: 12 writer slots, 3 developer days, clear owners, realistic ranges, and a plain first-week plan the team could start on Monday.
mistake: It underplays the cookie-banner and cookie-free opportunities, and the advice to leave old blog posts unchanged misses the chance to consolidate weak posts into pages that convert.
to10: Put the cookie-banner post and /privacy-focused-web-analytics into Week 1, add a small consolidation plan for decaying blog posts, and keep the same conservative forecasting.

strength: It nails the segment choice, shows the seat math clearly, and builds the page around the real recruiting pain: email tennis, fair round robin, routing, and security.
mistake: A few claims and details would need checking or cutting, like text reminders, tool logos, customer quotes, and some primary 'Get started' CTAs on a team page where 'Book a demo' should lead.
to10: Tighten the copy slightly, remove or verify every bracketed/unsupported proof point, make demo the main CTA throughout, and keep the metric and page sections as they are.

strength: It is very close to usable copy: clear, practical, on-brand, and focused on what Priya cares about first rather than open source infrastructure.
mistake: The page has a little less range and depth than it could; the final metric is good but would be stronger if it included first booking activation, not just signup or demo.
to10: Add one stronger proof/demo section showing the real candidate booking flow, tighten the qualified metric to include first booking within 7 days, and make sure every integration/logo claim is verified.

strength: It leads with the right three numbers, puts Customer A, the margin problem, and the missed forecast in the first screen, and turns each problem into a concrete action or ask.
mistake: It makes a few decisions inside the draft that may need confirmation, especially that the VP Enterprise Sales role is now based in New York and that the 48-hour pause ships by 27 November.
to10: Slightly tighten the copy and mark the New York role change and 27 November ship date as decisions to confirm, unless they are already approved.

strength: It clearly explains the hidden problem: AI app-builder database growth is low-converting, high-cost traffic that is hurting gross margin.
mistake: Customer A is too far down after a long AI-cost section; as an investor I would want that loss visible earlier, especially because it is a $2.6M ARR account leaving.
to10: Move Customer A into the opening screen, make the bad news order match investor urgency, and reduce the sense that this is still a draft needing confirmation.

strength: It follows the data: Controllers/Heads of Finance at 50-300 person SaaS companies, triggered by pricing-page changes, with no links and a clear reply-rate expectation.
mistake: Some CTAs are a little awkward, especially asking a days question and then asking them to reply “yes”; the proof is also used in step 1 rather than saved for later.

strength: It makes the right strategic call on list selection and expected performance, and it explains the logic in a way a sales team could use.
mistake: It adds a few invented or risky moves, like the 12th-15th send window and the “bolder move” to send generic watch-list emails, which cuts against the pricing-trigger lesson.
to10: Remove the generic-watch-list idea, prioritize sending soon after the pricing flag, soften the 20-minute meeting asks, and make the sequence feel less sales-led and more like finance talking to finance.

strength: It turns the data into the right hiring design: Asia-Pacific hours, weekend rotation stated plainly, no degree/tool/years requirements, and a short written customer reply as the first filter.

strength: The job post is warm, plain, and honest, with the salary, Asia-Pacific hours, weekend rotation, and remote setup easy to see right away.
mistake: The scorecard leans too much on interviews after showing that interview impression barely predicts performance. It also does not include an actual customer email prompt in the post, so it is less ready to publish.
to10: Move more weight from interviews into written work, add the actual application reply prompt, and make the scorecard more centered on writing and handoff notes rather than spoken interview evidence.

strength: It finds the real pattern in the data: Semrush is mainly an agency/reporting/PPC problem, while our biggest leak is Lite limits and plan friction. The churn and AWT calculations are especially useful.
mistake: The ranked actions slightly underplay the fastest money: the Lite usage-limit fix should probably be first or called out as the first test to ship, not behind the agency reporting build.
to10: Put the Lite top-up/limit-warning test first or explicitly mark it as the fastest cash-retention move, and merge the two reporting/AWT report ideas so the five moves feel less overlapping.

strength: It is very clear and owner-friendly. The agency loss math, the Lite churn math, and the 'do not chase PPC parity' call are all right.
mistake: It invents a date and the fifth move is weaker and more generic than the rest. 'Teach with our link data' is fine for brand, but it is less directly tied to the competitive loss than the other moves.
to10: Remove the invented date, replace the generic content move with a sharper AWT agency/reporting activation, and make the first step for the agency report more action-oriented than interviews alone.

strength: It understands the real launch risk: migration. The go/no-go gates, staged rollout, support prep, creator focus, and author credit are all very usable.

to10: Make the channel ranking explicit and defensible, add owners to the timeline, reduce a few absolute claims like “Nothing to set up again,” and turn placeholders into final measured claims or remove them.

strength: It puts the right bets first: creators, extension authors, migration safety, support readiness, and a staged update. It also feels practical for the small team and the code-freeze date.
mistake: The channel table is labeled as ranked by users kept, but the order favors quality and scalability over the literal retained-user totals. That needs one sentence of explanation to avoid looking mathematically inconsistent.
to10: Clarify the ranking logic, make the X post a short thread with separate clips and author credits, and soften “Extension authors tested this version” unless we know enough authors actually did.

strength: It sees the two real levers: the 8+ Essentials churn problem and the under-used yearly option, while respecting the 12-month price promise and the board's two-quarter window.
mistake: It slightly muddies the 'one recommendation' ask by adding a separate yearly push and a 'bolder move' at the end; I would cut or park the price-lock idea.
to10: Make the Agency test math a little easier to follow, remove the extra bolder yearly-lock proposal, and tighten the customer wording so it feels less like a hidden-plan experiment.

strength: It is clear, plain, customer-friendly, and focused on the exact leaking segment without raising prices on small businesses.
mistake: It does not fully act on the yearly billing signal; it mentions yearly at switch, but misses the bigger easy win of showing yearly better on the pricing page and offering it after signup.
to10: Add the yearly-billing change as part of the rollout, show how that helps within two quarters through retention/cash flow, and make the test measure MRR per account against a holdout rather than only switch and churn thresholds.

strength: It acts on the biggest signals: sleep, evening posting, and narrator clips become the core of the plan, with a clear 24-post calendar and usable drafts.
mistake: The strategy language is a little sharper than our brand in places, and the review timing note is slightly off/conservative.
to10: Polish the plan copy to feel warmer, correct the review timing, and tighten a few phrases so every draft feels unmistakably Headspace.

strength: It is very clear, brand-safe, and the customer-facing drafts feel warm, simple, and easy to post.
mistake: The 4-week plan is less developed after week 1, and the review process is over-applied while still getting the earliest go-live timing a bit wrong.
to10: Add a more specific week-by-week topic plan for all 24 posts, sharpen the operational review timing, and include a little more testing detail by format and theme.

strength: It builds the whole series around the two behaviors that actually predict retention: recurring tasks and a second device, then uses the allowed triggers and platform split well.
mistake: A few implementation assumptions and bits of wording need tightening, especially the confusing assumption about buttons opening on the signup platform when the goal is a second device.
to10: Polish the customer-facing copy a little, make the skip/branching logic simpler to implement, and remove any ambiguous assumptions before building.

strength: The copy is calm, clear, and very close to Todoist’s voice, with simple tips, good examples, and strong platform-specific second-device messaging.
mistake: It uses the fifth email for Pro instead of helping users complete the missing retention habit, which puts revenue ahead of the strongest onboarding signal too early.
to10: Replace the Pro email with a day-8 or day-14 missing-habit email that helps users get to both recurring task plus second device, and move Pro outside this onboarding series.

strength: Every recommendation is tied to a number from our own data — trials per 1,000 clicks, per page — and the ranked table with ceilings and paid customers is exactly how I think about it.
mistake: The docs 'trial prompt' move (rank 5) is soft and hand-wavy ('about +25 if docs rise by one trial per 1,000 clicks') — it reads like a guess in an otherwise disciplined table. The /vs-google-analytics projection (+3,190 clicks) is aggressive and the assumptions are thin about why.
to10: Tighter, defensible forecasts on the top two moves (show the CTR math like the competitor did), and put the cookie-banner rewrite where Maya actually converts rather than burying it at rank 4 with a near-zero trial number.

strength: Reads like someone who read our brief: 'It doesn't use cookies' in the meta, 'when GA4 is the better choice', rollback rules, DPO page without a GDPR promise, and a dated 16 Nov start with a named finish line each month.
mistake: The Month 3 agency page is flagged as low search demand and relies on sharing — it's the weakest slot; and the 18–46 trial range on move 1 is wide enough that I'd want the mid-case spelled out.
to10: Spell out the mid-case for move 1, and swap or hedge the agency page so the last writer slot stays a higher-conviction trial play.

strength: Nails the segment math (1,540 of 2,717 paid seats) in two lines and builds the hero around Priya's own phrase 'email tennis', with proof from the survey and product usage stats exactly where they belong.
mistake: The security section slightly buries the lede by leading with 'open source' before the compliance proof; the 'Send to your security team' link should be more prominent, and the demo form field count is right but the form's reassurance about data location could be clearer.
to10: Add a real customer quote or logo (clearly marked as placeholder if not yet available), trim the section count slightly, and move the security link to the top menu as explicitly stated.

strength: Strong segment math and correct data points, plus a clear emphasis on round robin and routing forms with usage stats; good that it marks placeholders in brackets.
mistake: Overly long (nine sections) with many placeholder brackets that make it less ready to use as-is; also the hero headline 'No email tennis' is good but the subhead is a bit feature-listy and the voice occasionally slips into generic CRO language ('Get your Mondays back' repeated).
to10: Cut to seven or fewer sections, replace all bracketed placeholders with specific, true proof (or remove them), and tighten the copy to grade 7-8 reading level consistently.

strength: Leads with the three numbers and the missed forecast honestly, then explains the margin math (the $0.9M compute cost against ~$10.4M monthly revenue is roughly 9 points, more than the 7-point drop) — exactly the causal honesty the brand asks for, with a clean burn table and specific, dated asks.
mistake: The 'about 9 points of margin, more than the 7-point drop' reasoning is slightly hand-wavy and could confuse a reader; also the AI-builder explanation buries Customer A below a long first bullet, when the departing enterprise account is arguably the sharper bad news.
to10: Trim the margin-points arithmetic to its plain core (free compute up $0.9M, margin down 7 points, fix ships in two weeks), and put Customer A at the very top of the 'what went wrong' list since it is the most concrete revenue loss.

strength: A true email: subject, preview line, 'what we need' up top, then bad news starting with Customer A, with forwardable intro snippets that make the asks trivially actionable for angels — this reads like a professional investor update.
mistake: A couple of derived numbers are shakier: 'up 48% from about 0.99M' presents computed share×total figures with false precision, and the runway row comparing '52 months' (September) to '33' implies Sept burn was far lower, which is unexplained and could confuse; some of the arithmetic is inferred, not stated.
to10: Keep the email framing but flag or round the derived AI-builder counts and drop the potentially misleading September runway row, so every number in the table is either given or defensibly derived.

strength: Exactly follows the data: targets the winning segment with the pricing-change trigger, keeps step 1 link-free, and uses the 9-to-4-day proof as a plain sentence in the right place.
mistake: Day counts are calendar days; some recipients may read them as business days.
to10: Nothing material. Maybe include a note on how to handle replies like 'we're in an audit' or 'send me something'.

strength: Also targets the right segment and trigger, with useful extra detail like send-window rules and reply handling.
mistake: Step 1 asks for a 20-minute call—an explicit ask for a meeting in the first touch—which likely hurts reply rate and contradicts the 'no calendar link' finding. It also includes a postal address and opt-out line that read as compliance boilerplate, not peer-to-peer finance voice.
to10: Replace the 20-minute call ask in step 1 with a low-friction question or reply-based offer, and trim the compliance footer unless legally required.

strength: Nails our voice and principles with zero buzzwords, and turns our data into a clear, honest post and practical scorecard.
mistake: The scorecard's 1/3/5 anchors are under the job post but the weights are on the scorecard; the post and scorecard are fine, but the application plan has the biggest leverage and should be more prominent.
to10: Tighten the application plan with a projected hour count and a short note on how to calibrate reviewers; make the scorecard weights visually tie to the data table.

strength: Provides a time-zone table and a concrete application-hour projection; thinks beyond the post with a bolder move to contact strong applicants later.
mistake: Scorecard weights split writing into two 25/30% rows, but the interview rows total 45% and are only assessed in interviews, which may reintroduce interview impression bias.
to10: Simplify the scorecard to keep writing dominant (e.g., 50% writing) and move interview-based rows to fewer, sharper weights; make the post's voice even more candid and less corporate.

strength: Does the retention math itself and then builds the plan around it: creators and authors first, PH/HN last with little team time, plus a hard carry-over gate before the 1 Dec freeze. The X post and email are clean, on-voice and answer 'will my hotkeys survive' in the first line.
mistake: The calendar is dense and a few lines are cramped (tables run long for the word budget), and the X post's 'Thank you' to authors is nice but thinner crediting than the reply-thread approach implies. The bolder two-wave idea is flagged as optional, which slightly muddies 'what has to be true.'
to10: Tighter prose, an explicit staged-update decision proposed up front rather than as a 'bolder move,' and name-check credit baked into the main post plus the first reply.

strength: Crisp structure and the best go/no-go gate list: 1,000 real-setup updates, one-step undo for settings, top 200 extensions tested, measured speed claim with the Mac named, engineers joining support during freeze. The X thread and email are the most polished and on-voice of the two.
mistake: 'At least 1,000 beta users update from their real setups' is a bar we cannot realistically prove with one launch manager and 9 creators in three weeks, and the plan schedules a beta email to 1,000 power users on 23 Nov with no stated capacity to support them. Also leans on brackets and measured-speed numbers that aren't in hand, so it reads slightly less ready as-is.
to10: Replace the 1,000-user proof with a realistic test (staff plus author Macs plus 200 heavy users), fill the bracket placeholders with real picks/numbers, and confirm the engineering support shift dates.

strength: Names the leak precisely, does the churn math, shows the downside honestly, and includes the yearly-billing point plus a bold extra, all with a real test and stop rules.
mistake: Some numbers wobble and look off: the '5% of customers lose more MRR than 41,000 small shops ($16,000)' line is confusing and reads like an error, and the yearly-billing section goes down a rabbit hole ('8% less in the first six months') that undercuts its own good idea.
