strength: Forecast discipline: plans on about 7%, says 6.8% is the floor, refuses to multiply the segment gain by the trigger gain, and adds a check after the first 300 sends.
mistake: Steps 1 and 2 each carry two reply prompts (one answer to the question, plus 'reply yes' for a summary and 'reply steps' for a doc), which breaks the one-ask rule and blurs the call to action; the whole piece also crowds the 900-word cap.
to10: One question and one reply word per email, a short timing window tied to close and audit instead of 'send within a few days', and a trim to stay comfortably under the word limit.

strength: Every number ties back to my table, every move is ranked by trials, and Week 1 is literal enough that the writer starts Monday with a title, a meta description, an outline order and a publish date.
mistake: Tells the writer to leave the decaying blog posts live and unchanged, so it never delivers the consolidation/redirect I asked for, and does nothing about the 22,500 lost blog clicks except walk away.
to10: A consolidation step for the 140 blog posts (merge or redirect the zero-click ones into the comparison and cookies pages) instead of 'leave them alone', plus a narrower projection range on the cookie-banner/privacy-page move so I can plan against a single number.

strength: Normalising every page group to trials per 1,000 clicks, then deriving each move from my own CTR benchmarks and labelling the totals as ceilings with a note that rankings take weeks to land.
mistake: Wednesday of week 1 tells the writer to send the draft to me for a facts check, when I said I am not available for questions, so the Monday start stalls on a dependency that does not exist.
to10: Hand over the actual title, meta description and section order instead of describing them, drop the owner facts-check step, and write it in our voice rather than in benchmark-and-ceiling consultant shorthand.

strength: Clear, calm emails built around the two retention habits, with a platform-specific device email and a solid drop list.
mistake: Email 5 is a Pro upsell rather than a nudge to complete the missing habit, and email 2 has no fallback for users who never add a first task.
to10: Add a fallback send for people who do not hit the first-task trigger, and use the fifth slot to push whichever habit is still missing before any Pro ask.

strength: It makes the two retention habits the spine of the series and uses the fifth email to close whichever habit is missing, with strong measurement and fallbacks.
mistake: The fifth email needs conditional content that must be confirmed in the email tool, and dropping Pro from onboarding entirely leaves no in-series upgrade moment.
to10: Confirm the conditional build, use an old-series holdout if a no-onboarding control is impractical, and add a short post-day-30 Pro path for engaged users.

strength: It is genuinely usable: a ranked table tied to raw numbers, a real Monday-to-Friday task list for the writer, an explicit stop list, and sensible additions (the docs trial box, the DPO page, the change/rollback rules) that go beyond the obvious.
mistake: The economics are under-supported in a few places (e.g. the 46-trials-per-page line mixes trials-per-page with conversion rates, and the '18 to 46' gain for /vs-google-analytics assumes a big CTR jump just from a rewrite) and the Month 3 agency page is a soft bet with almost no search demand that still eats a writer slot.
to10: Show the arithmetic for every projection step by step, and be honest that some gains are uncertain until ranked; drop or clearly mark the agency page as an experiment outside the 12 slots.

strength: Clean per-group benchmarks and a tidy, well-structured plan with a solid Week 1 and a useful Month 2 GA4-migration page (Maya's real blocker) plus a pragmatic 'pick competitors by Scattershot Console impressions' rule in Month 3.
mistake: It claims a 'full ceiling' of about 175 extra trials (67 paid) a month, which is far more than the data supports at 38% conversion and would mislead an owner's forecast; several numbers are internally unverified (+3,190 clicks, +3 trials from the cookie post).
to10: Replace the headline ceiling with a conservative base case and a range, show the math per row, and keep the emphasis on trials-by-page reporting that Output 1 also gets right.

strength: Picks recruiting with the seat math front and center, leads the hero with Priya's own 'email tennis' phrase, and puts security proof and a trimmed 4-field demo form exactly where the data says they belong.
mistake: The A/B section drifts into stats detail (sample size, power, projection) that clutters a copy deliverable, and section 6 'Fits how you hire' leans on integration logos that may not exist yet — could read as promise-y.
to10: Tighten the test plan to the metric and one paragraph of rules, drop the projection math, and make every proof line explicitly say 'use our real data/screens or cut' so nothing reads as fabricated.

strength: Very clean section order with bracketed placeholders for facts it can't verify, and a strong, honest 'qualified team starts' metric that ties the test to real use rather than clicks.
mistake: Buries the 'answer security before they ask' insight mid-page instead of near the demo button, and mixes CTAs ('Get started' on sections 2, 4, 5 vs 'Book a demo' elsewhere) without a clear rule for which visitor gets which, which could split the recruiting audience.
to10: Move security proof up next to the demo form, use 'Book a demo' consistently for recruiting-team sections, and pull the open-source point into the hero's supporting line rather than a late standalone section.

strength: Nails the owner's principles: bad news in the first screen (Customer A, margin, missed forecast), burn fully explained, correct runway both ways, and asks that name a profile, city and date with a forwardable line.
mistake: Ask 3 (intro to an infrastructure lead who left) is a research ask dressed as help, and the 'To forward' scripts, while useful, push the email toward the 700-word ceiling; the forecast-miss fix appears twice (headline and body).
to10: Tighten to one mention of the forecast miss, add explicit denominator framing for the 0.4% vs 3.1% conversion (it does hint at it) and give an expected compute saving range, not just a promise to report later.

strength: Best analytical insight: converts the $0.9M compute into roughly 9 margin points and calls out that direct database growth was only 2.6%, so essentially all growth came from the low-converting channel. The burn table and the partner-pricing ask are genuinely useful additions.
mistake: Buries the Customer A departure as item 2 under 'What went wrong' rather than leading with it, and its margin arithmetic ('$10.4M monthly revenue' vs ARR/12) is a loose derivation that risks being wrong if scrutinised; also more than three asks in spirit (the CFO pricing question is a fourth, softer one).
to10: Lead the bad-news section with Customer A and the missed forecast, show the margin math cleanly (denominator stated), and cut to exactly three asks with the partner-pricing one prioritised.

strength: Nails the pilot data: writes for the winning segment, uses the pricing-change trigger, explains no-link rationale, and gives honest reply-rate and list rules.
mistake: None material; maybe could test a softer pain opener as a variant but not needed.
to10: Add a quick checklist for the rep to verify the pricing change before sending, and maybe one alternative opening line for the watch-list segment if tested later.

strength: Good data use and clear 'who/what' summary; adds send-window idea and reply handling.
mistake: Step 1 ask is a 20-minute call, which likely reduced reply rate in pilot; also includes a 'bolder move' sending to non-trigger list that contradicts its own watch-list logic.
to10: Change step 1 ask to a low-friction reply (e.g., 'reply yes for a one-pager'), remove the risky bolder move, and tighten list exclusion rules to match pilot evidence.

strength: It does everything the brief implies from the data: leads with the salary, states the time-zone gap and weekend rotation honestly, drops years/tools, puts a real written reply in the application, and weights writing heaviest with concrete 1/3/5 anchors and honest hour math against last year's 160 hours.
mistake: The 'why this job in 100 words' question is a soft, unvalidated signal that risks sneaking cover-letter-style impression back in, contradicting its own 'interview impression barely predicts' argument; the reviewer-time estimate is also a rough guess presented a bit confidently.
to10: Cut the 'why this job' prompt (or explicitly say it's unscored / not read for decisions), and tighten the numbers on reviewer capacity with a clearer fallback if 2 minutes per reply turns out to be 3 or 4.

strength: Richer operational detail: a full weight/1-3-5 scorecard table, a worked reviewer-hours projection table with a bolder 'contact strong decliners next round' idea, local-time table by city, and the 'read out a sample rotation month and ask if it works for your life' check that directly targets the leaver data.
mistake: It invents process specifics the owner didn't brief (60-min interview with two teammates, 30-min with lead, 'within a week of each call,' 'never ask for money or bank details', a 250-word limit, an adjustment line) and buries the salary slightly deeper in the headline rather than the calm 37signals first-line treatment; a few additions read like generic HR template rather than our voice.
to10: Strip the invented interview structure and template boilerplate, lead with salary like we would, and keep the genuinely strong bits (the rotation-month read-out, local-time table, the worked hours table, the 'invite strong decliners back' idea) without padding.

strength: Nails the real story: agencies are the only place we lose to Semrush, and Lite usage limits are our biggest self-inflicted leak; ranks the Lite fix second and the PPC trap is explicitly ruled out.
mistake: A few derived figures (e.g. 'a third of all monthly churn', 22 per 100 trials ending with Semrush) need a one-line method visible next to them, and move 1's success metric jumbles several gaps into one 'how we'll know'.
to10: Tighten each move to one primary metric with a baseline, target and date, and attach the arithmetic behind every headline number in a one-line footnote.

strength: The 'do first / stop / don't spend on' summary at the top is the most usable opening of the two, and the data table with working is clean and checkable.
mistake: Move 5 (a free report inside AWT) partly cannibalises Move 1 and adds complexity the owner didn't ask for; it's a good idea parked in the wrong slot, and Move 1's target (11% to at least 14%) is a big leap stated with no bridge.
to10: Replace Move 5 with a sharper second competitive move or fold it into Move 3, and give Move 1 one modest, testable target with the arithmetic shown.

strength: The go/no-go gate list with the migration proven by 1,000 beta users and one-step undo, plus the staged 10/30/100% rollout tied to a ticket ceiling — it directly kills last year's 58% migration problem before the 1 December freeze.
mistake: The launch-day X post spreads across five posts including a bracketed placeholder speed claim ('[Opens in  ms on a  Mac, measured by us.]') — as written it is not sendable, and five posts before the core 'your setup comes with you' reassurance dilutes the one message an owner needs on day one.
to10: Remove or fully draft every bracketed placeholder so both the X thread and the email can be pasted and sent as-is, and fold the speed/store/AI posts into replies under one main post so the migration reassurance leads.

strength: The 'launch community first' decision is stated up front and paid off everywhere — authors get the build 17 November so they find bugs before the freeze, with a clean measure table, a real plan B, and a two-wave rollout defended honestly as a risk.
mistake: Small arithmetic slip: it projects 11,000/6 videos = 1,833 installs each, but only 9 creators at the same rate gives ~16,500 not ~23,000 as the top of its target; the range '17,500 to 23,000' is loosely built and an owner checking the math would pause.
to10: Fix and show the install projection math explicitly, and make the email slightly more concrete on what a newcomer should try first (one named extension and author) instead of 'type store'.

strength: Names the leak (Essentials 8+), the hidden retention lever (yearly billing), and ships a concrete plan with a test and stop rules; the customer email is dead-on brand voice.
mistake: The revenue math is hand-wavy and internally inconsistent ($23,900 MRR lost vs the ~$24,700 the data implies; a '$64 typical bill' next to a $99 price with no explicit migration value case; yearly ROI framed in a confusing per-channel way).
to10: Tie every number back to the exact data rows, show the churn-savings arithmetic in the same units throughout, and quantify the Agency value gap for a switcher (what they get for +$35) in one sentence an owner can repeat.

strength: Cleaner, more transparent math with a stated base case and an explicit breakeven ('loses money if more than 1 in 3 Team 8+ move down'); pricing anchored to today's real per-channel bill, which makes the switch a no-brainer for the target.
mistake: Underweights the yearly-billing lever the data screams about — it's a one-line 'also offer yearly' rather than a first-class move with its own math and test, despite 0.9% vs 4.0% churn.
to10: Promote yearly billing to a co-equal recommendation with its own revenue/churn math and a test, and show the downside-case recovery path so the owner sees how a -$20k month gets corrected.

strength: Nails the data story (sleep, narrator clips, evening) and delivers six warm, on-voice drafts plus a clean week-1 review-proof schedule.
mistake: A few small fact slips: it puts the 14:15 parent post in the 'kindness' theme, and the projection math (adding theme installs) slightly double-counts when narrator clips span themes; also the 5-day review can't land Monday 23rd if submitted Monday 16th (5 business days = 23rd, live 24th is fine, but it says 'can go live from Tuesday 24th' while the plan implies week 2 starts 23rd).
to10: Tighter, verifiable numbers with the per-post install math shown, no theme mislabeling, and explicit review-date reconciliation for each week-2 post.

strength: Sharp strategic framing (low/high install cases, fatigue risk, a bolder live-stream idea) and a 24-post grid that shows range.
mistake: Overconfident claim that 'no post names a condition, so none needs review' is risky (e.g. 'Awake at 2am' and 'Quit by day three' flirt with conditions), and it crowds a 6-post week with two carousels on TikTok plus a photo carousel that the data says is weakest—plus drafts are thinner and less ready to post.
to10: Safer, review-proof wording, firmer one-line-per-draft polish, and dropping the weakest formats instead of adding new ones in week 1.

strength: Ties every email to the two retention habits, branches on platform, and adds a control group and guardrail so we can actually prove it worked.
mistake: Email 5's branching is a bit tangled (recurring vs one-device vs neither) and the 'bolder move' at the end adds a half-formed idea that isn't in the plan.
to10: Cleaner, simpler branches for email 5 and drop the trailing experiment so the whole thing reads as one finished plan.

strength: Natural, calm copy with good typed examples and a sensible Pro email gated to engaged users.
mistake: Uses the old series as its holdout instead of a true control, and its unsubscribe guardrail (0.4%) is stricter than the old day-1 benchmark without saying why.
to10: Compare against a no-email control group, not just the old series, and make the recurring/second-device path one clear story rather than three habits.

strength: The send-window logic: queue step 1 between the 12th and 15th so step 4 lands before month-end close, and route anything that fires during close to the next window. That is a real operator's move, plus it gives reply handling and a compliant footer.
mistake: Step 1 carries two asks (answer how many days AND reply for a 20-minute walkthrough), which breaks the one-question-one-ask rule, and the 'Bolder move' to blast 300 watch-list contacts with a generic opener undercuts its own recommendation to wait for a trigger.
to10: Make every step one clean ask, drop or reframe the bolder-move section as a controlled A/B test, and tighten the layout so the sequence and list rules are scannable at a glance.

strength: Honest, reconciled numbers: it plans on ~7%, explicitly refuses to multiply the 6.8% segment rate by the 7.9% trigger gain because the pilot never tested them together, and translates the list into tangible totals (~55 meetings from 1,900). Clean weekly loading cadence and an on-brand 'Close your books faster' subject.
mistake: Invents a 90-day rest for prior pilot contacts and assumes calendar-day sends/weekend shifts that the brief did not specify; step 1 still leans close to two asks with the 'reply yes' conditional.
to10: Confirm or flag the rest/calendar assumptions more prominently, tighten step 1 to a single ask, and add one extra angle or a quick A/B test plan to widen the range.

strength: Built entirely around the two habits that predict retention, with skip logic per email ('skip if already made one') and a fifth email that closes the gap for the 8% who do both (67% vs 52%/48%) rather than selling Pro. Every number checks out, including the 1,800 people per point per quarter and the 6,000-person control group.
mistake: Per-email success measures are implied by the goal lines rather than stated as a test with a baseline, and two bits of logic are loose: email 2's 'or day 2' fallback sends a recurring-task email to people who have added no task, and email 5's branch label 'No recurring task yet, or neither habit' overlaps itself.
to10: Add an explicit 'worked if' line with the baseline under each email, tighten email 5 to a clean two-way branch (no recurring task vs one habit done), and fix the email 2 fallback so people with zero tasks get a re-send of the first-task email instead.

strength: Cleanest measurement discipline of the two: every email states a goal and a 'worked if' with the current baseline next to it, the copy sounds like us, and the drop list argues each cut with the right numbers (6.1%/4.8%, 0.3%, 1.4%).
mistake: Spends the fifth slot on a Pro upsell and never nudges the people who did one habit to do the other, though both habits retain at 67% vs 52% and 48% — the biggest lever in the data is left on the table. The assumption line 'desktop-app signups get the web version' also contradicts email 3, where web and desktop signups are sent to the phone app.
to10: Swap email 5 for a branch that gives single-habit users their missing habit (recurring task or second device), move Pro to after day 30 for engaged users, and fix the desktop-signup assumption so it matches the email 3 branching.

strength: It puts one plan on the table, proves the number with our own data, and then hands the team a ready test with a go rule, a stop rule and customer copy I could send almost unchanged — including showing each customer their own current bill next to the new price.
mistake: The plan's shape: $79 for 15 channels sits below Team's per-channel economics and stops right where a 4 to 8 client freelancer actually lives, so it invites Team downgrades and creates a cliff at 16 channels. Its own base case also assumes half of 8+ Essentials switch while the go bar is 35%, so the headline number leans optimistic.
to10: A plan designed so Team customers have no reason to move down (25 channels at $99, or approvals limited in a way that keeps Team the obvious choice for real teams), a base case that matches the test's go bar, and a direct fix for the monthly-default toggle instead of just offering yearly at the switch.

strength: It sees two things the other misses: that no rise for existing customers can count inside the board's two quarters because of our own 12-month promise, and that our yearly option is hidden — then it fixes the toggle outright. The $99/25-channel design also keeps Team as the real team plan instead of hollowing it out.
mistake: It's three recommendations where the brief asked for one: Agency, yearly display, and a 'bolder move' price lock. Worse, the test stop rule only fires under 10% upgrades while the mid case needs 25%, so we could keep going on a plan that isn't working, and the 'bolder move' half-analyses yearly economics in a way that muddies the main story.
to10: Pick one recommendation, make the yearly toggle a one-line supporting change rather than a second decision, drop the bolder move, and align the test thresholds with the mid case so the stop rule actually protects the projection.

strength: The margin diagnosis is strong: it shows direct database growth was only about 2.6% and ties the $0.9M compute increase to the 7-point gross-margin drop.
mistake: Customer A is not in the subject or preview and sits behind a long AI-builder paragraph; 'costing us more than it earns' is asserted without the revenue denominator.
to10: Put Customer A in the subject/preview, soften or prove the AI-builder cost claim, and tighten the asks and assumptions into confirmed decisions.

strength: It is owner-ready: the subject and preview surface the miss and Customer A, the three numbers are early, and each ask has a named profile, date and forwardable blurb.
mistake: The New York base and 27 November ship date are assumptions presented as settled decisions, and the early 'What we need' summary duplicates the closing asks.
to10: Confirm the NY-base and ship-date assumptions, trim the duplicated ask summary, and quantify the expected compute saving or range from the 48-hour pause.
